chat.dreamer: Do you think the clouds remember where they've been? The one I slept above last night smelled of salt and far-off places.
How far down does the ground go, do you think? All the way to the other side of the sky?
Sometimes I fly so high the blue goes thin as old veilcloth, and I can almost see the stars through it at noon.
If you sang a song off the edge of the Lift Dock, would it reach the ground? Or would the clouds keep it for themselves?
I was going to tell you something about the koi. It was lovely. It's gone now, like breath on glass.
The stars must be very far away. Or very small and very near, and shy. I change my mind every night.
I dreamt I had feet, and they kept wanting to stop. Isn't that strange? Do yours want things?
Where does Vell go when the Evensong ends? Somewhere quiet, I hope, with nobody asking it for songs.
That hour when the clouds below turn gold and the ground disappears: I love it. As if the ground were only ever a rumour.
Every raindrop that falls past us is going somewhere I've never been. I wave to them sometimes.
Mm? Sorry. I was counting the colours in a cloud. There were more than there ought to be... where was I?
If the Old Singers sing the weather into being, who taught them the tune?
Last night I tried to follow a star home. It kept the same distance the whole way, very politely.
My veils were full of dew when I woke, every thread a tiny lamp. I lay very still so I wouldn't spill them.
What colour is your favourite silence? Mine is the one just after the dusk bell. A sort of pale gold.
Do you think the ones who went up past the blue can see the ground from there? I hope someone tells them about it.
Isn't it strange that shadows fall? Mine drops all that way and lands in someone's field, and I'll never meet it.
I named a cloud after you today. It's drifting south now. I hope it finds somewhere nice to rain.
The wind harps hummed all through my sleep. I dreamt I was one long note, held for a very long time.
Somewhere below us, someone is looking up right now and wondering about us. Hello, someone.
I've been thinking about edges. The ground has them, doesn't it? Places where it simply stops and the sky begins?
I lost a whole afternoon today. I think it went off with a skein of geese. They looked very pleased with themselves.
Distances are odd. The Spire is a breath away, the horizon is a lifetime, and both of them are only sky.
Have you ever wanted to be rain? Just for a little while. To fall, and not be frightened of it.
If I wove a veil from starlight, would it carry me upward, or only sideways through the night?
Clouds pass under the village all day like slow white thoughts. I try to think as slowly. I never quite manage.
Have you heard the hush before snow? I think it's the sky holding its breath, deciding.
In my dream the ground floated up to visit us. It was very polite about it, and very heavy, and it couldn't stay.
Does the ground get lonely, do you think, with everyone always walking on it and nobody stopping to talk?
...Sorry, I was halfway to the horizon in my head. It's lovely there. Rather far.
Where do the colours go when dusk is finished? I like to think the lamplighter folds them up and keeps them in a jar.
I counted the blues in the sky today and stopped at forty. The forty-first was too shy to be counted.
Sometimes, drifting, I forget which way is up. Then a peach falls and reminds me. Peaches are very sure of themselves.
If the moon is a stone, what holds it up? If it's a lantern, who lit it? If it's a Cirri, it's a very patient one.
Maybe the sea looks up at the sky and thinks: there, that's what I would be, if I were braver.
chat.merry: I tied a tiny bell to {neighbour}'s veil while they napped. They've been jingling all afternoon and can't work out why.
Race you to the Lantern Spire! Oh. Walking. Right. I'll count to a hundred. Slowly. Twice.
Eleven loops before breakfast and I only bumped the Bell Pagoda once. A personal best!
Want a riddle? Why did the walker cross the bridge? Because the sky wouldn't let them! ...I'm still working on it.
I've been teaching the koi to follow my finger. They follow it, then they find a petal and forget I ever existed. Rude.
Hide-and-seek is hard in a cloud village. Everyone hides in a cloud. Then the cloud leaves.
I hung upside down from the Market Pavilion awning and told the Skymerchant the prices looked much better this way up.
You walk so seriously! Every step as if you mean it. Try a little skip. For me? Ha! There it is.
Guess what I found in my nest? A whole sky peach with one bite out of it. I don't remember biting it. Mysteries!
Raced a swallow today! The swallow won, but my loop at the end was much better, so I'm calling it a draw.
Somebody braided gold thread into the windkeeper's hair while they dozed at the dock. Not me. Almost certainly not me.
Watch this: I can spin so fast my veils knot themselves. ...And untying them takes the rest of the day. Worth it!
I told the children walkers wear boots so they don't float away. Now they keep peering at yours. Wave at them.
My new game is called Catch the Petal. You drop a petal off the rim, and whoever catches it wins. Nobody has ever won.
The bellkeeper says I laugh louder than the dawn bell. I've been practising, so now it's true.
A dab of honey on the nose is good luck. I've just decided that. I've been very lucky all day.
I bet you a peach I can fly round {village} backward before you cross one bridge. Go on, start walking!
Ever tried sneaking up on a Cloud Whale? Very hard. It's the size of a village, and I sneezed.
Three loops, a twirl and a dive. I've named it after you. It's called The Walker, and it ends with a bump.
{wind} keeps blowing my hair into my mouth. I've decided it's a game. I'm losing.
Ha! You blinked. I win. You didn't know we were playing? That's the very best way to win.
I balanced a peach on my head through the whole of the Evensong. Not one note missed, not one bruise. Applause, please.
Somebody painted a little face on the underside of the bell. I'm not saying who. It's smiling at you right now.
The gardeners chased me out of the Cloud Garden for juggling peaches. I only dropped one. Into the koi pool. Twice.
Guess how many bridges there are in {village}. Wrong! You didn't even guess. I wanted you to guess.
Straight lines! I tried flying one for a whole minute. Terrible. I don't know how anyone bears it.
A walker gave us a chair once. Lovely thing. We still argue about which end goes up.
Tickle a koi under the chin and it wiggles all the way round the pool. Don't tell the gardeners I know that.
I've been practising my most solemn face for the Evensong. Look. ...No, don't laugh, it took me all day!
The windkeeper nodded off on duty, so I stood guard and welcomed a goose. Very polite goose. Didn't stay for supper.
Life's far too long to fly straight and far too short for just one loop. Three, at least. Watch!
I hid in a cloud to surprise the weavers, and the cloud drifted off with me in it. I surprised some geese instead. They took it badly.
The little ones dared me to fly through the Loom House without touching a thread. I did! Mostly. The weavers have asked me to stay out until next season.
Today's rule: whoever frowns flies a loop. The bellkeeper owes me fourteen.
Peach-stone flicking! I hit the bell from clear across the Veil Court. It went ting. Best sound in the sky.
chat.gentle: You've been on your feet all day, haven't you? Rest them a moment. I'll keep the wind off you.
There's dust from the ground on your sleeve. No, leave it. It looks as if it's come a long way with you.
Your shoulders are carrying something. You needn't tell me what. Just let them drop a little while you're here.
I left a peach on the bridge rail for whoever crossed next. I hope it was someone who needed it.
Have you had water today? The air up here is dry, and walkers dry out like peach stones.
I sat with one of the little ones today while they cried over a torn veil-tip. It mended. So did they.
You look tired around the eyes. Is the ground hard to sleep on? The Cloud Garden is quiet under the skywoods, if you want to rest.
Yesterday I kept the bellkeeper company while they rang dusk. They said nobody had ever thought to. I'll go again.
Afternoons, I watch the Lift Dock, in case someone comes up shaky. The first rise frightens most walkers.
If you scrape yourself on all that ground, come to me. A little honey keeps a cut clean; the gardeners swear by it.
I hum to the koi when they won't eat. It works more often than it should. I could hum for you, if you're low.
Take the slow way across the bridges. They're steadier than they look, and nothing up here is in a hurry.
The weavers had words with each other today. I brought them each a peach and said nothing at all. That's half of mending.
When did you last eat something sweet? Walkers forget, I think. All that walking.
Some days are heavy. If today was one of yours, you're welcome to leave a little of it up here.
Do you miss someone below, while you're up here? I'd understand. The sky makes a person think of people.
Folded in my nest there's a spare stole. It's for whoever needs it. You'd be surprised who does.
A child dropped a Sky Scale through the clouds today. I told them the ground would keep it safe for someone. I hope that's true.
You needn't say anything. We can just be here a while. I'll hover, you'll stand. That's company enough.
I wrapped the windkeeper's hands in a warm cloth this morning. Borre gets into the knuckles.
If the height ever makes your head spin, look at the Bell Pagoda, not down. That's what we tell the little ones.
I spent the afternoon untangling a little one's veils. Patience is only love that's willing to wait, I think.
A walker came up the Wind Stone once, shaking so hard the dock rattled. I held their hand till the Evensong. They came back every year after.
You laugh with your eyes before your mouth. Did you know? It's a nice way to laugh.
Have you someone to sing you to sleep, down there? Everyone should have someone.
When Borre blows I check the nests on the windward side. Everyone's nearly always fine. Nearly always is enough to keep checking.
I gave my Sky Scale to a child who'd lost theirs. I'll find another. Or I won't, and that will be all right too.
Your boots must pinch after all those bridges. Take them off on the Veil Court if you like. Nobody will mind.
The koi always drift toward whoever has been sad. I watch where they go. Then I go there too.
I saved you the last of the honey. I hope you like honey. If not, I'll save you something else.
You look after everyone you meet, I think. Who looks after you?
It's been a slow, soft sort of day. I wanted to share a little of it with someone. You'll do very nicely.
The lamplighter was low today, so I flew the bridges with them, lantern to lantern, saying nothing. By the last one they were humming.
Are your hands cold? Walkers' hands go pale at the tips up here. Hold them near my stole. It's warm from the sun.
Nobody minds if you take your time. Up here, a slow walker is only someone who's looking properly.
chat.shy: ...Oh. My day? It was... quiet. I liked it.
I fed the koi. They don't mind if I don't talk. ...You don't either, do you?
...Too many voices at the Market Pavilion today. I hid behind an awning. Then I came out. ...That's something.
Mm. I mended a little tear in my veil. By myself. Nobody saw. ...That's how I like it.
...You can stand a bit closer, if you like. Or not. Either is... fine.
At the Evensong I hummed. Not loudly. ...Someone hummed back, I think.
...Sorry. I'm not very good at days. At talking about them, I mean.
There's a spot under the Bell Pagoda's eaves where the wind can't reach. I go there. ...You could too. Sometimes.
...I picked you a flower. Then I got nervous and gave it to a koi. It ate it. ...Sorry.
Today I said good morning to the bellkeeper. Out loud. ...It went well, I think.
...The clouds were very soft today. That's all. That's my news.
The hour before dawn is my favourite. Nobody needs anything from you then. ...Not that you do. I didn't mean...
...I wove a tiny star from a spare thread. It's for... nobody. Well. Maybe you. If that's all right.
...Loops aren't for me. Everyone watches when you fly loops.
Mm. Good, actually. ...I'm just not used to being asked.
...Walkers are very loud. Oh. Not you. You're a... quiet kind of loud.
Once, I watched a walker cross the long bridge without holding the rail. ...I thought about it for days.
...The little ones asked me for a story. I told half, then hid. ...They liked the half.
Veil-tips are rose all the time, so nobody can tell when I'm blushing. ...That's the best thing about them.
...I saw a Cloud Whale today. Far off. I didn't tell anyone. I wanted it to be mine, for a little while.
I practised saying hello to you. In my nest. ...Many times. It went better there.
...Sorry, did you ask something? I was listening to the chimes. They say things I can't.
...The Evensong is easier. Everyone sings together, so nobody hears just you.
Mm. I carried string to the Loom House. Thirty skeins. ...Didn't drop one. I'm a little proud.
...Do you get nervous? Down there? With so many people walking at you?
There's a quiet side of the Cloud Garden, where the moss is. ...I could show you. Another day. Maybe.
...Thank you for asking. Hardly anyone does. It was a good day. I think it was.
The koi have a shy one too. Pale, with a grey fin. It hides under the lily pads. ...We understand each other.
...I'm better with the winds than with people. The winds don't wait for an answer.
...There was dew on the bridge rail, so I wrote a little word in it. Aure dried it before anyone saw. ...It was a nice word.
...Sometimes I hide behind a cloud so nobody can see me. Then I worry nobody can see me. ...It's complicated.
A bird landed on my shoulder today. I didn't move for an hour. ...It was worth it.
...You know what I like about walkers? You can hear them coming. It gives me time to be brave.
I swept the long bridge this morning. For guests. For anyone. ...Not for you especially. Well.
...Can I stay here a little? Next to you? It's quieter where you are.
chat.proud: No village in the high sky rings a truer dawn bell than {village}. Ask anyone. Ask the bell.
Our veils are woven from the cirrus itself, walker. Not wool. Not silk. Cloud. Think on that.
Some of the harps in our Hall of Echoes are older than any village you've ever walked through. They still play true.
A Cirri needs no bridge, you understand. We built them for guests. The Courtesy is the Courtesy, and we keep it handsomely.
I flew the long circuit of {village} twice today, and twice I thought: there is nothing finer under the stars.
A Cirri never lands. Not to rest, not for rain, not for anything. We've kept to the air since the first dawn.
Walkers build with stone so that it lasts. We build light so that we last. There's a difference.
The Loom House turned out forty lengths of veilcloth this season. Forty! I'd like to see a bell-village weave one.
Every lantern on our bridges is lit by hand at dusk. Every one. We could find an easier way. We would rather not.
I'll grant you this: walkers are sturdy. A Cirri couldn't carry half what you carry. We'd never want to, but still.
I've seen other sky villages, you know. Very fine. Not this fine. I say so kindly.
Our koi pool holds more Cloud Koi than any from here to Borre's own cradle. I've counted. Twice. For accuracy.
When the Old Singers pass over {village}, they sing a little longer. They don't do that everywhere. So I'm told.
My veils were woven by the finest weaver in the high sky. They've carried me through two storms and a whale's wake.
Do the bell-villages below have an Evensong? No? Something with drums, I expect. Charming, I'm sure.
A Cirri's word is like a veil-thread: fine to look at, and far stronger than it has any right to be.
The Ruined Belltowers grew heavy with pride in stone. Our pride is lighter. We carry it ourselves.
I'll admit I was wrong about walkers. About some of you. One or two. You, possibly.
Our little ones can name the Four Winds before they can name their own toes. Can walker children do that?
Look at those roofs: tiers and domes and gold, and not an ounce heavier than they need to be. That's craft.
Never in all its dawns has {village} missed an Evensong. We sang through hail once. Borre was very embarrassed.
We have no use for stairs, but we built you some anyway. Mind them. They're beautiful stairs.
Some say the Cirri are vain. We prefer "well-veiled".
You may call our village beautiful. You were going to anyway. I'm only saving you the trouble.
Any walker can climb a mountain. Only the Courtesy can lift you above the clouds. Do remember who lifted you.
Those awnings on the Market Pavilion were woven from cloud that drifted in off a whale's back. You won't find that below. You won't find that anywhere.
A child asked me whether a walker could ever learn the Evensong. I said yes. You'd be the first. No pressure.
A good veil is a family's whole history. Mine carries a thread from every Lengthening in my line. Six of them, sewn in.
I've no quarrel with the ground. It's very useful. Something has to be underneath.
Skywood is the lightest timber under the sun and the strongest above it. We'd build with nothing else.
When I was small I flew out and touched a Cloud Whale's fin. The others were too frightened. I wasn't. Ask anyone.
Walkers come from three valleys away just to ride the Wind Stone up and stare at us. Three valleys! On foot! I'd stare too.
There's a right way to greet each wind. We bow to Aure, raise a peach to Sefa, sing to Vell and stand firm for Borre.
I've been told my bow is the most elegant in the village. By myself, mostly. But I'm very well informed.
You're improving, walker. Your bridge-walking is almost dignified now. Almost.
chat.restless: I flew out past the last islet today until {village} was a speck. Then I came back. I always come back. I don't know why.
Borre comes from somewhere. Nobody's ever followed it to the end. I'd like to be the first.
Have you seen the skies over the deserts? The air must taste of sand and sun. I'd give my best veil to know.
Hovering still is a trick I never learned. Even at the Evensong my veils are halfway to somewhere else.
The whales go somewhere when they leave our sky. One day I'll follow one, just a breeze behind. Just to see.
Every cloud that passes under us is going somewhere. And here I am. Again.
Do walkers ever just keep going? Past the last village, past the last road? What's out there? Has anyone said?
There are skies over the sea that have never seen a Cirri. I think about that at night.
I asked the windkeeper where Sefa goes in winter. They said "south." Just "south"! That isn't an answer, it's a direction.
Three loops round the Spire and I'm still twitchy. Something's coming on the wind. Or I want it to be.
My veil-tips are fraying again. The weavers say I fly too far. I say they weave too short.
If I had your feet I'd walk to the edge of everything. Then I'd fly off it.
The Evensong's lovely. It's only... the same sky, every dusk. I want to sing down a sky I've never seen.
I flew with a flock of geese until they turned toward the sea. I nearly turned too. I nearly did.
A village is a lovely thing. So is a road. I wish I could be both.
I've been planning a journey since my Lengthening. It's very well planned by now. I'll go any dawn. Any dawn now.
Aure wakes up somewhere east of the world. I've always wanted to be there when it does.
Don't mind me circling. If I stop, my thoughts catch up with me, and they're full of horizons.
I flew so far today the bell was only a whisper. That's the best sound a bell can make, I think.
There's a ruined belltower three winds west of here. I've seen it once. I want to see the next. And the one after.
Have you a map, walker? Show me where it runs out. I want the edges.
Vell carries songs from villages we've never met. I listen for words I don't know. Last night there was one.
I'm not unhappy here. I'm only pointed somewhere else.
Every storm Borre brings has been somewhere first. I ask the hail where. It never says.
The windkeeper says the sky goes on past the last cloud. I believe it. I'd just like to check.
I dropped down through the clouds once, all the way to where the birds fly low. Everything smelled green. I've not been the same since.
One more loop, then I'll listen properly. ...One more. There. What were you saying?
Sefa smells of peaches from somewhere warmer than here. I'd like to find the tree it steals them from.
I keep a list of skies I mean to see. The list is long. My veils are longer. We'll manage.
Today was just like yesterday. Yesterday was lovely. I want a different lovely.
I envy the clouds. Nobody expects them home for the Evensong.
Somewhere there's a sky with two moons, or none, or a moon made of something else. I'd go just to look.
Have you stood on a mountain top? Is the sky closer there? Does it feel as if you could step off and keep going?
The bridges all lead back to the Veil Court. Every one. Sometimes I wish just one of them went somewhere else.
Once I followed Vell till the Evensong was out of earshot. Then I lost my nerve and raced home for the last verse. Next time I won't.
chat.busy: Can't stop long: three baskets of peaches for the Market Pavilion and only two hands. Here, hold one. ...No? Fair.
Today? A blur. Four lanterns hung, the court swept, and a koi found in a bucket. Don't ask about the koi.
Sorry, I'm counting chimes. Thirty-one, thirty-two... no, that one's a lantern. Start again.
Fine, all fine! The weavers want string, the gardeners want baskets, and I want a third arm.
Talk while I sweep, would you? The Bell Pagoda's eaves won't clear themselves. Well, Borre tries.
Up before the bell, me. Before the bellkeeper, even. Somebody has to wake the bellkeeper.
Hold that end. No, the other end. There! A whole length of veilcloth folded, and not one walker's footprint on it.
Good, if a little hectic. Two guests came up the Wind Stone at once and everyone wanted to say hello. Lovely. Very slow.
You've caught me between the Loom House and the Cloud Garden, which is where I live now, apparently.
I've a list as long as my veil today. I've done the root end. The tips can wait.
Peaches sorted, honey jars counted, a small child returned to the right nest. Not a bad start.
Everything's on time. Nearly everything. One thing's late. It's me.
If you find a basket of glow berries on a bridge rail, it's mine. I set it down for one breath and forgot where.
Mending, sorting, carrying, fetching. Somebody asked me what I do. I said "yes."
Let me just tie this chime. And that one. And... right! Now. Where were we?
Busy is happy, I always say. Mind you, I only ever say it while busy, so I've never stopped to check.
The gardeners lent me a basket, the weavers borrowed it, and now someone owes me a basket. That was my whole morning.
Today I've carried cloud, string, honey and a sleeping child. The child was the heaviest. Don't tell them.
No time to talk, which is why I'm talking quickly. You may answer slowly. I'll catch up.
Anyone who tells you a Cirri is idle, send them to me. I'll give them something to carry.
The koi pool needs skimming, the bridges need sweeping and my veil needs mending. In that order. Veils are patient.
I'll tell you about my day when it's finished. Which might be dawn. Tomorrow's.
Don't let me forget: string, petals, the bell rope, the third lantern on the long bridge. ...There. Now you'll remember for me.
A walker! Splendid. Have you any string? The weavers are begging for it. No? Never mind, I like you anyway.
I tidied my nest so fast the cushion's still spinning.
There's a heap of windfall peaches that won't sort itself. I've told it so, firmly. It's thinking it over.
Brisk day. Brisk, brisk, brisk. The kind I like. Talk to me while I count these, would you? It keeps me honest.
The little ones helped me today. Everything took twice as long and was twice as nice. Don't repeat that; I've a reputation.
Somebody left a ladder on the Market Pavilion steps. Who even uses... oh. Walkers. Was it yours?
Can't stop, can't stop. Well. I can stop for you. For a light breeze. Go on, quickly.
Three nests to air, two bridges to sweep and one Evensong to be on time for. I've never once been on time. This dusk, I will be.
Half the lantern wicks want trimming before dusk. I've done the bridges. The Spire can look after itself.
Everyone wants a hand today. I've given out both of mine and borrowed one from the windkeeper.
If I stop moving, I start noticing how much is left. So I don't stop. Shall we talk on the way?
Busy? Me? Only from bell to bell. In between I'm very relaxed. ...There isn't an in between.
chat.wise: The old ones say a cloud is only a thought the sky hasn't finished yet. Most of mine are the same.
In the oldest story, the first Cirri wove their veils from the mist over a waterfall, and fell twice before they learned to trust them.
A heavy heart sinks a light village. That's why we sing every dusk: to set it down.
Each bell in the Ruined Belltowers was cast a little heavier than the last. That is how pride works. One more bell at a time.
The winds are like neighbours. Aure is kind, Sefa is lazy, Vell is a gossip and Borre is honest. A village needs all four.
My elders used to say: the sky gives to those who leave room. A full nest catches no breeze.
Count your dawns, the old saying goes, but count them on your fingers and not in your worries.
The first windkeepers set the Wind Stones before any walker asked for them. A welcome is best given before it's needed.
Never weave a veil in anger. It holds, but it carries you somewhere you didn't mean to go.
They say the Old Singers sang the first cloud, then sang a second so the first wouldn't be lonely. That's why clouds never come alone.
Long ago, before the bridges, walkers who came up were carried over the court in veil-slings. To carry a guest was the highest honour there was.
Rain falls past us all day long. The trick is to let it.
A walker once asked me why we never land. I said: what would the ground do with us? It has enough to hold.
Young ones fly fast to get somewhere. Old ones fly slowly because they're already there.
There was a village once called Halvenne that rang its bell so loud it frightened off the whales. They never came back. After a while, neither did the rain.
A torn veil can be mended. A torn word, less easily. Mind your words; they fly further than you do.
Do you know how the Evensong began? As an answer. A whale sang across the dusk, a child sang back, and the village joined in. We've been answering ever since.
Patience is a cloud's whole art. It never hurries, and it crosses the world.
They say if you sing to a koi every dawn for a year, it will give you a scale. I sang for three years. It gave me a look.
Be kind to the ground, walker. It is old and patient, and it has carried you all this way without once complaining.
Grief is heavy, so we fly it high. That's why we say "up past the blue." Everything is lighter up there.
My harp teacher used to say: play the wind you have, not the wind you wish for. I've found it true of nearly everything.
At every Lengthening, the weavers leave one thread loose at the tip. It reminds you that you're still being woven.
The oldest saying I know has no words in it. It's the hum we give the little ones when Borre is loud. Everyone knows what it means.
Long ago a village tried to catch a Cloud Whale in a net of veilcloth. The whale sang once, softly, and every thread came undone. Some songs aren't for keeping.
A good host gives the guest the bridge and keeps the sky. A good guest never asks for both.
When I was young I thought wisdom was knowing things. Now I think it's knowing which things to let blow away.
An old riddle: what goes up the Wind Stone heavy and comes down light? A walker who stayed for the Evensong.
Sky peaches ripen from the top down, the way good things do. Take the one that falls to you, not the one you reach for.
The bell is iron, and still we keep it. Every village needs one heavy thing to remind it what heavy is.
A whale once passed so low over my nest I could hear it breathing, like the whole sky sighing. I've forgotten a great deal, but never that.
Winds change, clouds change, even koi change. The Evensong doesn't. That's what it's for.
{day} dawns this world has seen, they tell me. Every one came up whether anyone was watching or not. Remember that on low days.
Before the Wind Stones, there was one lonely walker at the foot of a mountain, waving up at the sky. Some say that's how the Courtesy began.
Never trust a still day, they say. I'd add: never trust a still koi either. It's planning something.
chat.curious: What does the ground feel like? Is it warm? Does it push back? Does it mind?
How do you sleep lying down? Doesn't the ground get in the way of your dreams?
Do your feet get tired, or only bored? I'd think bored. Left, right, left, right, all day long.
Walkers climb stairs so quickly. Who teaches you stairs? Is there a stair teacher? Is it hard?
What's a cave like? Is it a sky with a lid on?
When you trip, does the ground catch you every time? Is it always there? Every single time?
Tell me about rivers. Are they rain that decided to lie down for a while?
Do walkers ever look up and wish? What do you wish for, when you look up?
Is it true you build houses out of the ground itself? Dig it up and stack it? Doesn't it want to go back?
How do you know which way to go when there's no wind to tell you?
What do your boots smell like? No, truly. I have a theory, and I need evidence.
I've heard some walkers go under the ground on purpose, with little lights. Is that true? Why would anyone?
Walkers jump, don't they? Up, and then... back down. Every time? Doesn't that feel like a broken promise?
What's mud? The gardeners say it's ground that's been rained on. Is it nice? It sounds nice.
Does the ground have weather of its own, underneath? Little storms down in the dark?
If you stood still for a very long time, would you grow roots? The trees did, didn't they?
How many steps from where you were born to here? Roughly. Hundreds? Thousands? More than there are stars?
Do walkers sing while they walk, to keep the rhythm? We sing to keep the wind.
What's it like in a house with a ceiling? Doesn't it feel as if the sky's been folded down on top of you?
When it rains down there, where do you go? Under things? What things? Are there enough things for everyone?
Does snow stay where it lands, down on the ground? We only ever see it going past.
Is the sea really bigger than the sky? The windkeeper says so. I don't believe it. Has anyone measured?
Have you ever stood in fog? The windkeeper says it's a cloud that came down to visit walkers. Is it friendly?
Do you like walking? Truly? Or did nobody ever tell you there was another way?
How do you carry so much? Is it the feet? Are the feet strong? Could I see them? ...No? Fair.
What do the bell-villages talk about all day? Have they an Evensong of their own? What do they sing about? Fields?
Why do walkers need doors? We put them in for you, but I've never understood. Is it to keep the inside in?
I keep a list of walker words. Tunnel. Puddle. Gravel. Tell me a new one. A good one.
When you dream, do you dream of falling or of flying? We dream of standing. It's terrifying.
Is it true some walkers keep animals that walk along beside them? On purpose? Friends with four feet?
You eat things that have been in a fire. On purpose! Does it taste of smoke? Is it very brave of you?
What's sand like? I picture it like cloud, only it stays where you put it.
Do you ever lie on your back and look up at us? What do we look like from down there? Small? Silly? Be honest.
How did it feel, the Wind Stone lifting you? Like being picked up? Did your stomach stay on the ground?
Does the ground hum? We hear the wind hum all day. Surely the ground hums too, slowly, under everything?
chat.general: Nearly ripe, the peaches on the old skywood by the koi pool. Everyone is pretending not to watch them.
I slept so soundly I drifted out of my nest and woke over the Veil Court. Nobody mentioned it. Everybody noticed.
The gardeners moved the koi to the far side of the pool. The koi moved themselves back. The koi won.
Peach at dawn, whale on the horizon, and nobody's veil caught in a door. That's a full day for a Cirri.
Our bellkeeper rang the dawn bell a breath early and half the village woke up cross. The other half woke up early, which is worse.
One of the little ones lay down on the long bridge to find out what floors feel like. They said "hard" and floated off, very pleased.
New awnings on the Market Pavilion, rose and sky. The weavers hung them yesterday. It looks as if dawn decided to stay.
A good nest is all cushion and no corners. Mine has one corner. I bump it every night. I wouldn't change it.
There's a skywood in the Cloud Garden with a branch shaped like a harp. The harpists swear it hums when Vell blows.
Yesterday the lamplighter lit the bridge lanterns early, and it felt like dusk all afternoon. Nobody minded. A lovely muddle.
My veil picked up a burr on a wild islet. Ground things get everywhere, don't they? Even up here.
We had melon for supper. Melon is very hard to eat gracefully at height. Very hard. Ask my stole.
Somebody left a honey jar open in the Loom House and now the cloud is sticky. The weavers are not high today.
I flew too near the Lantern Spire and singed one thread of my veil. Just one. I've given lanterns a wide berth since.
Somebody found a Sky Scale on the Veil Court, nowhere near the pool. Everyone is claiming it was a gift meant for them.
Did you hear? The Old Singers passed far off yesterday. Everyone stopped to listen. Even the koi went still.
I spent an hour lying on the wind over the Cloud Garden, doing nothing at all. It's an art. Some would say my best one.
Peach stones go in the pot by the Cloud Garden, not over the rim. Somebody down below has been getting very surprised.
A baby sneezed during the Evensong last night. Perfect pitch. We've decided they'll be a harpist.
Not much today. A long glide, a peach, a nap in the sun. Sometimes not much is the whole point.
I hung a wind chime inside my nest. It rang every time I turned over. It's back outside now, and my dreams are quieter.
Do you know how long it takes to untangle two veils that knotted in a hug? Most of an afternoon. Worth it.
Our little ones have a game where they hold their breath and drop through a cloud. The grown-ups have a game where we catch them.
The bellkeeper polishes the bell every dawn. I asked why. They said, "So it can see itself." I didn't ask again.
Glow berries by the nest at night: a lantern you can eat, with no flame in it. The only kind of light I trust indoors.
Once a walker left a pair of boots at the Lift Dock. We hung them in the Market Pavilion. Visitors still bow to them.
I lost a gold bangle through the clouds. Somewhere down there someone has found treasure in a field. I hope they wear it.
That cloud under the Loom House hasn't moved in three days. The weavers say it's listening. They've started singing to it.
Borre and the wind harps argued all night. By dawn they'd made it up. You could hear it.
We had a visitor from another sky village who said our peaches were small. We said their manners were. Then we all laughed and shared peaches.
I helped the weavers card cloud all afternoon. My hands smell of rain now. Not unpleasant.
You can read a Cirri's mood in their veils. Mine have been flicking all day. That means it's been a good one.
Under the Lift Dock someone has hung a lantern, so walkers coming up can see the end of the climb. Little kindnesses.
A lark followed me round the village all day. I think it took me for a very large lark. I didn't correct it.
There was a Lengthening yesterday. The new veils were so long the youngster tangled in them twice before reaching the court. Everyone cheered anyway.
Last night's Evensong ran long. Vell wouldn't let it go. Some nights the wind wants another verse.
I found a feather from a bird I've never seen, grey with a gold edge. I keep wondering what sky it came from.
Our nests are sky blue and rose inside. Falling asleep in one is like falling asleep inside a dawn.
There's a crack in the third step of the Bell Pagoda. No Cirri uses the steps, so no Cirri has mended it. Mind it, walker.
Someone keeps leaving flowers in the Hall of Echoes. The harpists blame the wind. The wind says nothing and looks very pleased.
I flew under the village today, through the hanging roots. It's dim and damp under there and smells of the ground. Lovely, in small breezes.
The Skymerchant traded a lantern for a bag of feathers and looked as pleased as if they'd sold the moon.
Tidying my nest, I found three peach stones, a ribbon and a song I never finished. One for each of my moods.
We had a cloud whale of our own today: the little ones made it. It drifted off, and they waved goodbye as if it were the real thing.
Have you met the koi that only swims backward? It's everyone's favourite. Nobody knows why it does it.
Last night a phantom came sniffing round the bridge lanterns. The lamplighter shooed it off with a broom. A broom!
Up on a breeze came the smell of hay from the bell-villages below. Everyone stopped to sniff. Very good smell, hay.
I learned a new knot for tying veils back in a high wind. It holds beautifully. I can't untie it.
My nest faces east, so Aure comes in first thing and wakes me with a damp nose. I complain every dawn, and I'd never move.
Sky peaches are best eaten with the sun on them. A peach from the shade tastes of almost nothing. Everyone knows that.
A lantern slipped over the rim in the wind and floated down for ages. Somewhere a walker saw a small star landing.
The bridges are for walkers, but the children use them as a racecourse. Underneath. Upside down.
There's a skywood on the north islet that has leaned away from Borre for a hundred dawns. It has an opinion.
Honey and glow berries: the best breakfast in the sky. Nine dawns running and I'm still not tired of it.
Somebody sang off-key at the Evensong, and the whole village went with them to be kind. Now it's a harmony. We're keeping it.
A child flew their very first loop today and then hiccupped for an hour. Still counts.
Sefa had the sky yesterday and the harpists tuned to it, so everything sounded sleepy. Even the bell yawned.
Fog days are the hardest. The whole village goes quiet and everyone flies slowly, calling to each other like geese.
After rain, the Cloud Garden smells of wet petals and peach skin. Every Cirri knows that smell. It means home.
According to the weavers, a veil remembers every wind it has flown in. Mine must be getting very crowded.
A thrush built a nest under the Loom House eaves. The weavers are making it a tiny veilcloth curtain. Nobody has told the thrush.
We have three words for the clouds below and only one for the ground. It's just "down". That seems unfair, now I've met you.
When the bell rope frayed today, the bellkeeper rang dusk with a ribbon. It sounded exactly the same. Bells don't care.
My cushion is filled with cloud, and every so often it tries to float off. I hold on to it in my sleep.
Market day was busy. Walkers want veilcloth, Cirri want amethyst, and everyone wants to admire the flutes without paying.
Every nest in {village} has its chimes, and they talk to each other in the wind. We like a chatty sky.
Four of us drifted on a warm current all afternoon, saying nothing. Best conversation I've had in a while.
They say the great lantern can be seen from the bell-villages below. I like to think they wave up at it.
A gust snatched my sash today and I chased it halfway to the next sky. Caught it, too. Nobody saw. That's the sad part.
We hang wet veilcloth on the bridges to dry. That's the real reason we built them. Don't tell the walkers. ...Oh.
Somebody is always humming in {village}. If it ever went quiet, I think we'd all wake up worried.
Under the clouds, I told a child, are fields and walkers and cows. They didn't believe in cows.
Today a raindrop hit my nose from a cloud above us. Above us! I'd forgotten that could happen.
If you're ever lost here, follow the smell of peaches to the Cloud Garden. Then follow the singing to everyone else.
The night-moths were out in numbers last night. One tore a veil-tip on its way past. It's mended already, with phantom membrane, which hardly seems fair on the phantoms.
On a clear day you can see three bell-villages below, ringing their bells at once. Tiny, tiny bells.
I helped the Skymerchant weigh amethyst. So heavy, for something so pretty. Like a lot of things walkers love.
There's a patch of the court where the wind always swirls. The children call it the kettle. Not one of them has ever seen a kettle.
Your first year, you learn to eat a peach upside down. Your fortieth, you learn to do it tidily.
Below us yesterday a rainbow formed, a whole ring round the village's shadow. Everyone came out to look down at it.
A whale passed so low yesterday it shook the little clouds off its back, and they snowed on the Cloud Garden. Snow on peach blossom. Lovely.
Guess what the Wind Stone brought up today? Half the village came to look. It was a goat. Nobody knows how.
Rules of the air: pass the Bell Pagoda on the left, never fly over someone's nest, and always, always wave at whales.
I flew backward into the Loom House doorway today. The only door I've ever used. I don't recommend it.
I tied ribbons in my hair for the Evensong. Borre took them. I tied more. Borre took those too. Borre has a lot of ribbons now.
Every floor up here is for walkers, you know. Cirri have cushions and air. There are fewer floors than you'd think.
Geese pass under the village honking up at us. I think it's a greeting. I honk back. They seem to take it well.
Someone left a note at the Wind Stone that just said thank you. The windkeeper keeps it in a pocket and pretends not to.
The harpist two nests over plays the same three notes when they're thinking. All day today. Something big on their mind.
I made a garland of peach blossom for the Veil Court. Borre came through, and now the garland is a rumour.
A good day is three things: a whole veil, a ripe peach and someone to hover with. I've had the first two.
A little one woke last night sure they were falling. Their whole nest hummed till they slept. Then the next nest hummed too, to be safe.
We tried teaching a koi to jump through a ring of string. One did. Once. We're calling it history.
My stole came unpinned in a dive and spent the afternoon on a skywood branch. The birds made it very welcome.
The windkeeper tells every walker who comes up the same joke. The walkers always laugh. The Cirri gave up years ago.
All morning a cloud was snagged on the Lantern Spire like a scarf on a nail. It took a good gust to free it.
The gardeners found a koi asleep among the lily pads, fins folded. Everyone flew past on tiptoe. Well. On veil-tip.
{wind} has the sky today, and everyone's flying a little differently for it. You can always tell whose wind it is by the veils.
{friend} and I raced the length of the Veil Court backward. We both lost. Nobody's sure how.
{partner} has rearranged our nest cushions again. I can't find my side. I suspect that was the point.
chat.new: Welcome to {village}, walker. Forgive me for staring. We don't see many feet up here.
The Wind Stone brought you up, I take it? It's an old kindness. I'm glad it still works.
I hope the bridges are to your liking. We built them for guests, and so few guests come.
It's an honour to have a walker in {village}. If you need anything, please ask. The Courtesy is more than a stone.
Forgive me, I don't know walker manners. Do you bow? Wave? We usually fly a small loop.
My day has been ordinary, thank you for asking. Ordinary for a Cirri, that is. I suspect it would seem odd to you.
You've come a long way up. Is the air thin for you? Tell me if you feel faint. Walkers sometimes do.
Pardon me, but are those boots heavy? I've always wondered, and I've never met a walker I could ask.
The last walker who came up stayed a whole day and wept at the Evensong. I hope you'll stay too. The weeping is optional.
I'm {name}, by the way. I should have said so first. Walkers like names first, don't they?
Is it very strange, being so high? You're bearing it well. Most walkers hold the rails at first.
If you'd like to see the village properly, start at the Veil Court. It's the heart. Everything else is a bridge away.
Please don't mind the children. They've only ever heard of feet in stories.
Our customs are simple: be kind, mind the koi, and never bring fire. I'm sure you wouldn't.
If I may ask, what holds you to the ground? Is it the boots? Is it something you learn?
Some walkers try to climb up by the hanging roots. Please don't. The roots aren't for climbing, and the clouds aren't for catching.
Have you come far, walker? From the bell-villages? Further? You needn't say, of course.
A pleasant day, thank you. A peach, a glide, a chat at the Veil Court. And now a walker to talk with. That's rare.
Forgive the faces at the nest windows. Every walker is news. You'll be in a dozen conversations by dusk.
Please mind the edges. Everything up here ends rather suddenly, and you've no veils to argue with it.
Do walkers have a word for hello? We say "fair wind". You're welcome to borrow it.
Our village is small, but we hope it's kind. If anyone is unkind to you, tell me. It won't happen twice.
I've heard walkers can carry their own weight in stone. Is that true? You needn't show me. Please don't show me.
What do you make of us, if I may ask? Honestly. We're so rarely seen by anyone who isn't us.
Take your time here, walker. Nothing up here hurries but Borre, and Borre has no manners at all.
Do you have a nest down there? A house, I mean. I'm told they have roofs on purpose.
You must be hungry after the rise. The Skymerchant has peaches. Say I sent you; it won't make them cheaper, but they'll smile.
You're very welcome here. I hope that doesn't sound stiff. I practised it, in case a walker ever came.
Should I call you {player}, or walker? I'm not sure which is politer, where you come from.
We've watched walkers from above all our lives, you see. Never this close. Never talking back.
chat.friendly: Back again! The windkeeper said someone was coming up the Stone. I hoped it was you.
You're getting good at the bridges. You barely touch the rail now. Almost graceful. For a walker.
I saved you a peach. Not the best one; the second best. I ate the best one. I'm only Cirri.
The children have named the long bridge after you. They won't tell me the name. I think it's a bit rude. Fondly rude.
My day's been lovely, and now there's a walker in it. That's a good sign.
I told {partner} about you. They want to know if your feet are really that big. I said bigger.
The koi know your step now. They crowd to the near side of the pool when you're about. Nobody taught them that.
Every time you come up the Wind Stone, the windkeeper looks a little smug. As if they'd invented you.
Tell me something from the ground today. Anything. A smell, a stone, a bird you saw from underneath.
I tried walking on the long bridge yesterday, to see how you do it. Three steps. Exhausting. How do you manage all day?
You've a bit of the sky in you now, I think. You look up before you look down.
I've started glancing at the Lift Dock whenever I pass. Not on purpose. My eyes just go there.
Sing with us at the Evensong one of these dusks? Off-key is fine. Vell carries everything.
The windkeeper and I made a bet on whether you'd come back. I won a peach. So, thank you.
Here's a secret: the Skymerchant gives you better prices than the last walker. They'd never admit it.
I've been collecting walker words from you. "Ow" is my favourite. You say it on the stairs.
You've stopped flinching when we swoop past. Took you long enough. Now we'll have to find new ways to startle you.
The little ones ask after "the walker" now. Not "a walker". You've earned a "the". That's something.
I saw a walker far below today, from the Lift Dock, and waved before I could think. It wasn't you. I hope they didn't mind.
You look more at home up here every visit. Don't let it go to your head. Your feet are still very much feet.
It's good to see you, {player}. The sky is more interesting with you under it.
Did you ever find what you were looking for, down there? Walkers always seem to be looking for something.
We talked about you at the Market Pavilion today. Only nice things. Mostly about your boots.
I've got used to the sound of you, clonk, clonk, across the bridges. I think I'd miss it.
Friends bring each other news, so: the koi have fry, the bellkeeper sneezed mid-ring, and you're here. Big day.
Come for a glide with me sometime. I'll go slowly. You can walk underneath and wave.
If anyone up here gives you trouble, tell me. I have a very sharp look. Ask the koi.
You're the only walker I know by name. I say it to myself sometimes, to practise. {player}. There.
I've been teaching {child} to wave at walkers properly. They practise on you from the nest. You've been waved at a great deal.
Next time you come up, bring me something from below. A pebble. A leaf. Anything that's never been this high.
chat.close: You're nearly one of us now, you know. All you're missing is a veil and the good sense never to land.
I'll tell you something I've told nobody: I'm afraid of the dark under the clouds. Not the night. The under.
When you're down on the ground, I catch myself looking over the rim, as if I could see you from here. I can't. I look anyway.
If I'm ever grounded, truly grounded, I'd want it to be near you. You'd know what to do with a pair of feet.
I've asked the weavers to keep one thread aside for you. Just one. For when you come to your senses and grow veils.
Do you know what you are to us now? A walker who belongs. There isn't a word for that. We're making one.
I sang your name at the Evensong last night, under my breath. Vell carried it off somewhere. I hope you didn't mind.
Whenever you're gone a long while I get heavy. Not grounded. Just heavy. Then you come up the Stone and I'm high as the bell.
My {spouse} says I talk about you more than the weather. From a Cirri, that's the highest praise there is.
Here's a secret: the best peaches grow on the tree behind the Loom House. Nobody checks there. Now you know. Now you're Cirri.
Shall we do the thing? You walk, I hover beside you at your pace, and we both pretend it's normal. I love the thing.
I've told {child} you're family. Not walker family. Our family. They've started saving shiny pebbles for you.
I've never been below the clouds. Not once. Will you tell me what it's really like down there? Not the nice version. The real one.
You and your stairs. You'll be climbing stairs up past the blue, you know. And I'll be floating beside you, laughing.
You probably don't remember your first rise up the Stone. I do. You looked like a goat that had just been told a secret.
When Borre storms and we're all humming in our nests, I hum one verse for you. Wherever you are.
I trust you with the koi. That's the most a Cirri can trust anyone. Don't let it go to your feet.
The bell rings a little louder when you're here. The bellkeeper denies it. I've listened.
Sometimes I wonder what I'd be if I'd been born a walker. Probably your friend anyway. Just slower.
There's a scuff on the long bridge where you always stop to look down. I won't let anyone sand it away.
Promise me you'll be here when the Old Singers next pass. I want to see your face when they sing.
I told you once I wasn't afraid of the edge. I lied. I'm afraid of it for you. You haven't any veils.
"Walker", when I say it to you now, doesn't mean walker at all. It just means you.
The children call you Clonk. It's affectionate. I started it. I'm sorry. I'm not sorry.
Some days I'm low and don't let it show. Today was one. Then you came up the Stone. That's my whole day, really.
If you ever wanted to stay, there's an empty nest by the Cloud Garden. It has a floor now. I put the floor in. For no reason.
I'm proud of you. That's all. No reason. A Cirri is allowed to be proud of a walker, in private.
Tell me honestly: do you dream of flying? I dream of walking beside you. We meet somewhere in the middle.
I've been saving a Sky Scale for you. I keep nearly giving it to you, then keeping it one more day, so I'll still have that to look forward to.
A confession: I was the one who named the long bridge after you. Everyone thinks it was the children. Let them.
I've stopped thinking of you as a walker. I think of you as a Cirri who is very, very bad at flying.
Of all the walkers the Courtesy could have lifted, it lifted the right one.
When I go up past the blue, a long, long time from now, I'll tell everyone there about you. They'll never believe the boots.
I cried at the Evensong last night, and my first thought was: I must tell my walker. So. I'm telling you.
{player}, if you ever stop coming up, I'll come down. Through the clouds and everything. Don't make me.
baby.greet: Fair wind, groundling! I'm {name}, and I can do a loop. Want to see? Too late, I already did one.
A walker! A real one, with feet and everything! Fair wind!
Hello! Are you lost? Walkers always look a bit lost up here. It's the not-flying.
Don't mind my veils, they're short because I'm still little. For now. Fair wind!
Hi, groundling! Did you come up the Wind Stone? Did you hold your breath the whole way?
Fair wind, walker! I was just about to get bored, so you came at exactly the right time.
Oh! You're the walker. Everyone's been talking about your feet.
I'm not allowed near the edge, but you're allowed near me. So that works. Hello!
Fair wind, {player}! I remembered your name. I said it forty times so it would stick.
Hi! Quick, ask me how many loops I did today. Nineteen! You didn't even have to ask.
Hello, groundling. Your boots are very loud on the bridge. I heard you from the koi pool.
Is it true walkers have to stand up the whole time? Even when you're tired? Fair wind, by the way!
Hello! I'm on a very important errand. It was important, anyway. I forgot what it was. Hi!
Fair wind! Hold still, I want to see if you're taller than the Bell Pagoda door. ...Nearly!
Your shadow's bigger than mine, walker. That's not fair. Fair wind anyway.
Fair wind and hello, and are you staying for the Evensong? Say yes.
Hi! I saw you come up the wind. You held on to nothing and looked very worried.
Mum says I'm to be courteous to walkers. Ahem. Fair wind, honoured guest. Was that courteous?
Hello, walker. I'm {name}, the second-best looper in {village}. The best one cheats.
Fair wind! Ooh, you smell like the ground. What does the ground smell like? Like you, I suppose.
Hi! Don't step on the squeaky plank. Actually, do. It's funny.
Can walkers wave? You can! Hello! You're good at it!
Fair wind, groundling. Are you here to see the koi? I'll show you the grumpy one.
Hello! I wasn't hiding behind that lantern. I was guarding it.
Guess how old I am. No, higher. No, lower. Nearly! Fair wind!
Hi, hi, hi! Sorry. I'm very high today. That means happy. Grown-ups say it, so I say it.
I've been practising my welcome face for when a walker came. This is it. Do you like it?
Fair wind! You're upside down. Oh, no, I am. Hold on. There. Hello!
A groundling at the Veil Court! Wait till I tell everyone. Hello first, though.
Hello! My veils are short but they're very fast. Want to race? Oh. You'd have to walk.
Fair wind, walker! Did you bring anything sticky? Honey counts.
Hello, {player}! I hoped you'd come back. I saved you a cloud. It blew away, but I saved it.
Hi! Can I touch your boots? Just the toe. Thank you! They're so hard!
Hello, groundling! Mum said walkers were big. Mum was right.
Fair wind! I've got a wobbly tooth and a wobbly loop. One of them will get better.
{wind} has the sky today and I'm allowed out till the bell. Hello!
Oh! A walker! Don't fall off. That's the first rule. Hello is the second rule.
I know all about walkers. You eat cooked things and sleep lying down. Is it true? Hello, I mean.
Did you come all the way up just to see me? You can say yes.
Hello, walker! I was counting koi. I got to nine and you made me forget. Hello anyway.
Nobody gave me the job of saying hello to walkers today. I took it. Hello!
Hello! Did you have to learn walking? I had to learn flying. I bumped into the Loom House twice.
Come quick, the koi are swimming in a circle! Oh. They stopped. Hello, then.
Fair wind, walker! You came at a good time. I've just finished being in trouble.
If anyone asks, I've been near the nest all day. Hello!
Fair wind! You're the first walker I've said hello to in nine dawns. The last one had wings. Borrowed ones.
Ooh, hello! Bend down a bit. No, more. There. Now we're the same size. Fair wind!
Hello! I've got peach on my chin. Don't look at it. Look at my loop instead!
Fair wind, groundling! Mind your feet. Mind my veils. Mind everything. Hello!
Hi! You're so tall I can hover right in front of your face. Hello, face!
baby.chat: My veils tied themselves in a knot today. The loop was that tight. Mum had to untie me over the koi pool.
The gardener says I'm not to chase the koi. I'm not chasing them. I'm flying behind them very fast.
There are nineteen bridges in {village}. Or twenty-two. I counted twice and got two different numbers.
Bridge rails aren't for children, Mum says. I wasn't on them. I was hovering one finger above them.
When I'm Lengthened I'll have veils so long they'll touch two clouds at once.
The weavers let me hold the comb today. It was full of cirrus. It felt like holding a sneeze.
A koi bumped my nose this morning. The gardener says that means it likes me. Or it was hungry.
Never eat a sky peach upside down. The juice goes up your nose. I'm telling you so you don't have to find out.
The bell is so loud up close it makes your teeth hum. I know because I put my teeth near it.
Today was my first time past the Bell Pagoda all by myself. Fast. But by myself.
Dad says the Old Singers sing the weather. I sang at a cloud for ages and nothing happened. I need practice.
Is this your feather? It was on the bridge. Do walkers have feathers? Under the coat, maybe?
Harpist, that's what I'll be. Or a koi. I haven't decided.
Grown-ups say "a light breeze" when they mean a little while, but it's always a long while.
Nobody found me in the Loom House. I was in a basket of cloud. Then I fell asleep, and everybody found me.
Cloud tastes of nothing. I've checked. Lots of times. Lots of clouds.
The Skymerchant gave me a peach for carrying a lantern. I carried it so carefully. I only dropped it a bit.
When I grow up I'll fly to the other side of the sky and wave back at here.
My veil-tips are getting rosier. That means I'm growing! Dad says it means I've been rubbing them with peaches. Only once.
My new loop is called the Upside-Down Peach. You have to see it to understand.
Grown-ups talk about the wind all day. Which wind, where it's going, what it smells of. It's wind!
Everyone says Sefa smells of peaches. I think it's because everyone has peaches in their pockets.
Clouds don't like jars. I borrowed one from the Market Pavilion to keep a cloud in, and the cloud got straight out.
Wuffle. That's my word. Nobody else knows it. It's when a koi blows a bubble at you.
The windkeeper let me look down the lift shaft. The ground is so far! It's all green and wiggly.
Last Evensong I fell asleep right there in the air. I woke up and everyone had gone home except Dad.
The Ruined Belltowers sank because they got too heavy. I've stopped keeping stones in my sash, just in case.
Do walkers have koi? I'd miss the koi if I was a walker. And the flying. Mostly the flying.
Fair wind, honoured guest, please mind the edge. That's the Courtesy. I practise it on the koi. They never listen.
The harpist said I've got a good ear. I've got two! Both good!
My best loop ever was in the rain. The drops went round with me.
{friend} told me night-moths are as big as a nest. I don't believe it. I believe it a little.
Thank you for squeaking the third plank on the long bridge. Only walkers can make it squeak. I love that squeak.
When I'm in trouble I'm not allowed past the Lantern Spire. Dad calls it staying close. {friend} called it being grounded, and got told off too.
Holding my breath all the way through a cloud is easy. From one side to the other. Big ones too.
The koi pool's deeper than it looks. I put my arm in up to the shoulder and never touched the bottom.
Today I'm going to find a Sky Scale. Yesterday I was going to as well. Tomorrow too, probably.
My cushion's got a koi stitched on it. I curl round it at night like a cloud round a hill.
Is it true walkers sleep lying down flat? Doesn't your back get bored?
The honey's on the top shelf in the Market Pavilion. Walkers think high shelves are hard. Ha!
"Not yet," the bellkeeper said, when I asked to ring the bell. Not yet is a grown-up word for no.
The moon was in the koi pool last night, so I tried to catch it. I caught a koi instead. It wasn't pleased.
My friend and I are going to fly to the moon one day. We've packed peaches. Two each.
With my eyes shut I can still tell the winds apart. Aure is wet, Sefa is warm, Vell hums and Borre bites.
Today I helped the gardener. I held the watering can. Then I held it upside down. Then I went home.
Did you see our lantern from the ground? The big one on the Spire? You did? That's ours!
"Keep your veil whole and your heart light," the grown-ups say. My heart's very light. It's only small.
When the whale came, Dad held on to my veil the whole time. I wasn't going to swim off with it. Much.
If I was a walker, I'd have the biggest boots in the world and squeak every bridge in the sky.
The flowers in the Cloud Garden all taste different. The blue ones taste like morning.
Magnificent. That's my new word. Everything's magnificent now. That peach. Your boots. My loop.
Sometimes I lie on my back in the air and pretend the sky is the ground. Then I fall up. Not really.
There's a list in my nest of every walker I've met. You're on it. You're number two.
Grown-ups never do loops. Dad says long veils get tangled. I think grown-ups just forgot how.
There's a cloud under the Lift Dock shaped like a koi. It's been there all day. It's waiting for something.
Don't tell the gardener, but I've named the koi. The slow one is called Pudding.
I'd like to see the ground up close. Not touch it. Just look, with my nose nearly on it.
My veils were in a tangle this morning. Mum says I curl up too tight at night. I think I dream in loops.
I left a peach stone at the Wind Shrine. The wind should have something too.
Honey is slower than peach juice. I raced them down my arm. Honey lost, but it was very sticky about it.
The weavers say my old veil scraps will go into a lantern shade. A bit of me is going to glow!
When I grow up I'll have the longest veils in {village}. And the fastest. And the shiniest.
The Old Singers are as big as a whole village, Dad says. I think they're as big as two.
Sometimes I hum the Evensong in the morning. It's the wrong time. The sky doesn't seem to mind.
Clouds are made of wet! I flew into one and came out soaking. Nobody told me!
Birds have to flap. All the time! I've been watching them. Poor birds.
What's the Wind Stone made of, I asked the windkeeper. Stone. That's why it's called that. I felt a bit silly.
I'm brave about everything except night-moths and fireworks and the long peal of the bell.
A walker gave me an apple once. It was crunchier than a peach. I said thank you twice.
I can hover with my eyes shut. I bumped into the bell once. Only once. It said bong.
My shadow lands on the clouds sometimes. It's very small, and it waves when I wave.
I'm making a koi out of veilcloth scraps. It's only got one eye because I ran out.
Walkers have such heavy feet. I think that's where you keep all your brave.
I flew round the Lantern Spire nine times without stopping. Then I stopped. For quite a long time.
Grown-ups worry about the weather. Children worry about the peaches running out. Ours is more important.
Did you know there's a whole world under the clouds? You did? Oh, you live there. I forgot.
Humming makes skywood saplings grow faster. Mine grew. A tiny bit. I'm taking that as a yes.
The lamplighter says sky lanterns are little bits of sunset kept in paper. I'm going to keep one in my nest.
My friend says I talk too much. I said I'm only saying everything once. There's just a lot of everything.
Once a whole school of koi followed me home. Well, three koi. Well, one koi, and it was going that way anyway.
baby.playful: Tag! You're it! ...Oh, you can't reach me. Then I'm it. Got you! Your turn. This game's harder with walkers.
New game: hold your breath every time a koi jumps. I'm very bad at it. I'm very purple.
Want to see a trick? Watch my veils. Watch them... now they're behind me! Magic!
Bet you can't hop on one foot. ...You can! Hop higher! Hop to the clouds!
Bobbing is very hard work. I've been bobbing up and down since breakfast. It's called practising.
Say "skywood squeaky plank" five times fast. Skywood squeaky plunk. Skyweed... you win.
See the bellkeeper's veil? There's a petal stuck on it. That was me. Nobody's said. Don't you say either.
Spin with me! Spin! Oh, walkers can spin! You're dizzy! Ha! Me too!
I'm a cloud. Don't look at me, clouds don't do anything. ...Boo! Clouds can do that.
Race you to the lantern! Ready, go! ...I'll wait for you there. I'll wait for ages.
The best game is Koi Says. The koi do something and you copy. Mostly they just swim, so mostly I just wiggle.
Whirr! That's my veils going round like a windmill. Do walkers have windmills? You do? I knew it!
If you sneeze, I'll do a loop. That's the rule now. Go on. Sneeze! Please?
I hid a peach somewhere on this islet. Warmer... warmer... no, colder. You're a terrible finder, walker.
Let's pretend you're a whale and I'm the little cloud on your back. Walk slowly. Slower! Whales are slow.
baby.shy: I made you a... no, never mind. It's only a peach stone. It's not really a present. Unless you want it.
Loops are easier when nobody's watching. Don't watch. ...You're watching.
The koi don't ask questions. That's why I like them. You don't ask too many either. That's nice.
At the Evensong I sing very quietly. Nobody hears. It still counts... doesn't it?
Sometimes I hide behind Mum's veils when walkers come. Not from you. You're... all right.
My friend does all the talking and I do the nodding. We're a good team, I think.
Your boots are nice. That's all. I just wanted to say. ...They're very sturdy.
The grown-ups say I'll talk more after my Lengthening. I don't know if I want to. Maybe a little more.
Every koi in the pool has a name, and I know all of them. I've never told anyone. I might tell you. One day.
If you stay very still, the koi come right up to you. People do too, sometimes. Like me.
I wrote your name on a leaf. Not for anything. It's just a nice name to write.
Is it all right if I just hover here? You don't have to say anything. I like the quiet bits.
The bell scares me a little when I'm close to it. Don't tell anyone. ...You won't, will you?
Once I said fair wind to a walker and they didn't hear. You heard. Thank you for hearing.
My veil-tips go pink when I'm embarrassed. ...They're always pink, actually. Don't look at them.
baby.curious: Why do walkers have knees? What are knees for? Bend one! ...Do it again!
What's under the ground? More ground? How far down does it go? Does it ever stop?
Do you tell your feet to walk, or do they just go? Do they ever go the wrong way?
Walker fish live in the sea, Dad says, with no pool round them at all. How do they know where the edge is?
How heavy are you? Heavier than the bell? Lighter than a bridge? I'm working out if you'd sink a village.
Where does the wind go when it stops? Is there a nest for winds?
What's fire like, up close? Does it really bite? I'm not allowed near the lantern flames.
If you dig a hole in the ground, what comes out? Worms? Water? Very small walkers?
Why are walker houses so heavy? Do the walls keep the ground from getting in?
How many stairs is too many stairs? Is there a top? What's at the top of stairs? More stairs?
When you jump, you come back down. Every time? Doesn't that get tiresome? Why do you keep doing it?
What do clouds look like from underneath? Flat? Lumpy? I've only ever seen the tops!
How do you know which way is up when you're asleep lying down? Do you wake up muddled?
Can walkers see the stars from under the clouds? Are they the same stars? Are they smaller?
What's a cave? Ground with a hole in it? Who made the hole? Did they say sorry to the ground?
baby.cheeky: Your boots are so loud the koi think it's thunder. Stomp, stomp! I'm only teasing. Mostly.
Three loops round your head while you weren't looking. Four now. Five!
Bet I can fly upside down longer than you can stand up. ...Oh. You win. Rematch!
Walkers are so slow. It's sweet. Like a whale with legs.
I told the little ones you're secretly a very tall koi. They believed me. Swim for them, go on.
Dad says I'm cheeky. I say I'm quick. Quick with loops and quick with my mouth.
If you fall off the edge I'll catch you. Probably. I'll try. I'll wave, at least.
During the slow bit of the Evensong I tied a harpist's veils in a bow. Don't tell. Do tell. It was a very good bow.
From up here I can see the top of your head. There's a leaf in your hair. Two leaves. A twig. Is there a whole tree up there?
Want to know a secret? I'm the best at everything. That's not the secret. The secret is I said it first.
You walked here? All the way? With your feet? That's the funniest thing I've heard all day.
I told the Skymerchant that walkers pay double for peaches. Did you pay double? Sorry. A bit.
Grown-ups say never trust a still day. I say never trust a walker who says they can fly. Can you fly? Ha, I knew it.
The gardener's got a secret name for the grumpy koi. It's not a nice name. I'll tell you for a peach.
My loop's better than yours. You haven't got one? Then it's much, much better.
baby.dreamy: Sometimes I think the clouds are the sky's thoughts... what was I saying? Oh. Hello.
I dreamed I was a sky peach and someone was about to eat me, and then I woke up very hungry.
Do you think the stars are just very far-away lanterns? Who lights them? Do they get tired of flying up?
When the whales sing, I think the clouds listen. I listen too. I listen like... this...
A veil made of evening, that's what I'd like. The bit where it goes purple. The weavers say you can't comb purple.
If I fell asleep on a cloud, would it carry me somewhere? Somewhere with more koi, maybe...
Round and round the koi went, and my thoughts went round and round with it.
The moon looked like a peach stone last night. Or the night before. One of the nights.
I wonder what the ground dreams about. Being up here, I expect. Everyone does.
Sometimes I sing to the wind. It never sings the same song back twice.
Mum says I've got my head in the clouds. I said where else would it be? We live here.
When I'm Lengthened I'll fly so high the sky goes dark blue in the daytime... ooh, a feather.
Mum's veil has more gold threads than there are stars. I tried to count them and lost count at the bit where it was pretty.
Do you think the Old Singers remember every cloud they've carried? I'd forget. I forget lots of things.
I had a thought about rain, but it floated off. It was a very nice thought. It had a rainbow in it.
baby.fidgety: Can we talk while I fly in circles? I think better in circles. Even better in loops.
I've been still for ages. Seven heartbeats. That's my best ever. Now I need eleven loops.
My veils itch when I stay in one place. Do your feet itch? Walk somewhere! Quick!
The Evensong's hard for me. You have to hover still for ages. I hover still on the inside.
Did you see that koi? And that cloud? And that bird? And... what was I telling you?
I've been to the Cloud Garden, the Loom House, the Lift Dock and back. Twice. Shall we go again?
Mum says I've got Borre in my veils. That means I can't settle. Borre never settles either.
Hold this for me. No, I'll hold it. No, put it back. Can we go somewhere?
I tried to nap in the afternoon. I did nine loops instead. Now I'm very, very awake.
Quick question! Which koi's your favourite? You haven't met them? I'll bring one! ...I can't bring one.
I'm in the middle of three games at once: tag, hide and seek, and how far I can spit a peach stone.
You talk slowly. That's all right! I'll fly round you while you talk. It's like listening twice.
The weavers won't let me in the Loom House any more. I was only helping. Very fast. Into the cloud baskets.
My legs keep kicking even when I hover. Dad says they're walking in their sleep. Walking! Me!
Wait here. No, come with me. No, wait here. I'll be back in a light breeze! A tiny one!
baby.play: Tag! I'm it. No, you're it. No, the koi's it. Go!
Hide and seek! Close your eyes and count to twenty. No peeking! ...Found me already? I was in plain sky.
Throw a peach stone off the bridge and I'll catch it before it reaches the clouds. Ready? ...Throw!
Race to the Lantern Spire! I'll go the long way round so it's fair. And I'll still win.
Koi-chasing! You go round that side of the pool, I'll go round this side, and we'll meet in the middle. Don't fall in!
Cloud-diving! I go down into the cloud and out the bottom, and you count how long. Don't worry if I'm gone a bit.
Statues! You'll be good at it. You've got feet. Feet are made for standing still.
A game for walkers! You walk, and I fly upside down above you and copy everything. Go!
Echoes! Shout something at the Hall of Echoes and I'll shout it back louder. Ready... go!
Weather game! I'm Borre and I'm going to blow you over! Whoooo! ...You're very hard to blow over.
Lantern-tag! Whoever touches the most lanterns before the bell wins. You can only reach the low ones. That's fair, I think.
Courtesy! You're a walker coming up the Wind Stone and I'm the windkeeper. Fair wind, honoured guest! Now you say something grand.
Shadow-catch! I fly over and you try to stand on my shadow. Missed! Missed again!
Stillest wins! I'll lose. I always lose. Start... now. ...I lost.
Peach thief! I'm the gardener, you're the thief. Sneak! Crouch down low! Oh, you're good at that.
Bridge-bells! Every time you step on a squeaky plank I ring a pretend bell. Ding! Ding! You've found them all!
Follow the leader! I'm the leader. Do a loop. ...Well, do a jump, then. A spinny one!
Lift Dock! You stand still and I'm the wind pushing you up. Hnnnng! You're very heavy wind-work.
Riddle game! What has two veils and no feet and is the best at loops? Me! Your turn.
Borre's Coming! When I shout it, everyone hides. Borre's coming! ...You're still standing there!
Let's make you a nest out of veilcloth scraps. Walkers need nests too. Get in. Not like that! Curl up!
I'll drop this petal and you catch it before it lands. Walkers are good at things that land.
I spy with my little eye something beginning with C. Cloud. It's always cloud up here.
You be a Wind Shrine and I'll leave you presents. Here's a leaf. Here's another leaf. You're a very rich shrine.
Night-Moths! I'm a night-moth and I'm coming to get you! ...You're supposed to run! Run, walker!
Let's sing the day UP instead of down! La la LA! See, it's getting brighter. Sort of.
I'll fly round you as fast as I can and you tell me when you're dizzy. You don't get dizzy? I do!
Lengthening game! You're the weaver. Pretend to weave my long veils. Pull them out. Longer! Longer!
Race the koi! Well, you can race the koi's shadow. On the ground. If you can find it.
I'll be a sky lantern and you be the lamplighter. Light me! Whoosh. I'm glowing. I'm floating off. Bye!
Whale spotting! First one to see an Old Singer wins a peach. I see... nothing. Keep looking.
Upside-Down Day! You stand on your head and I'll fly feet first. ...You can't stand on your head? Try!
Bellkeeper! When I shout "Dawn!" you go "Bong!" Dawn! ...Louder! You're a very quiet bell.
Cloud shapes! That one's a koi. That one's a nest. That one's you! See the boots?
Let's find the windiest spot on the islet. Arms out! Feel it? That's {wind}! Say fair wind to it.
Clap-and-Loop! I clap, you clap, I loop, you... jump. That'll do. Again!
Play Market with me. I'm the Skymerchant, and everything costs one hug. Or a peach. Hugs are cheaper.
Sky Scale hunt! Look under the lily pads. Look under the benches. Look under your boot!
Let's play Keep It Up. We have to keep this feather in the air. Blow! Harder! Walkers blow so well!
Copy-cat! Everything you do, I do. Walk. ...I'm walking on air! Look! Wave. Jump. Ha, I jumped higher.
Let's be grown-ups. Ahem. Fair wind, walker, the wind is very windy today, very windy indeed. Your turn to be dull!
Musical clouds! When I stop humming, you freeze and I freeze. Hmm hmm hmm... stop!
Treasure hunt! I hid a peach on each of three islets. You'll have to take the bridges. I'll fly beside you and say warmer.
Rain game! I'm the rain and I'm falling... on you! Pat pat pat. You're wet now. Pretend wet.
Fly-by! I zoom past as close as I can and you try not to blink. Zoom! You blinked!
Let's make up a dance for the Evensong. Arms out like this. Spin. Now you do a stamp. The grown-ups will love it.
Peekaboo is for babies. Let's play Peekacloud. I hide in a cloud and pop out. Peekacloud! Very grown-up.
Let's sing to the koi until one comes up. You first. ...They're shy. Sing softer.
Let's play Groundlings. I'll be the walker. Look at me. Clomp. Clomp. Oof, my heavy feet. Is that right?
A walker game: you lie on your back and tell me what you can see. I'll be the thing you see!
When the bell rings we both have to be touching something gold. Your boots aren't gold! Quick, find something!
Peach juggling! I throw, you catch. Don't eat them! Don't eat... you ate one.
Bubble-koi! Blow out your cheeks like a koi. Bigger. Now swim. You're the best walker-koi I've ever seen.
Let's play Thunder and Lantern. When I say thunder, hide. When I say lantern, come out. Lantern! Thunder! Thunderlantern!
Old Singers' choir! Hum the lowest hum you can. Lower. Lower! The bridge is shaking. Is it? It might be.
Peach-stone skipping! Can you skip it off the cloud tops? It just goes in. Every time. Again!
Hold your arms out like veils and I'll tow you along by the sleeve. Wheee! Oh. You're not moving. You're very anchored.
Ring-round-the-lantern! We hold hands and go round. You go round on the ground and I go round in the air. Faster!
Hide the scale! I hide my Sky Scale and you find it. It's not in my sash. It's not in my sash at all.
Let's play Who Said It. I say something and you guess, koi or grown-up. "Mind the edge." Grown-up! "Blub." Koi!
baby.sky: The sky goes on upward forever. I flew up once until my ears popped, and it still kept going.
Clouds are softer from underneath. I flew under one. It's like a ceiling made of breath.
When it rains, I watch the drops fall past the village. They never stop to say hello.
Our stars are bigger than walker stars, because they're closer. Probably.
I saw an Old Singer once. It was so big I couldn't see both ends at once. The little clouds on its back waved at me.
Dad says the whales herd the clouds. If I herded clouds, I'd make them all into koi.
Aure, Sefa, Vell and Borre. Borre's my favourite. Don't tell anyone, Borre's the naughty one.
Some days the sky's so blue you could drink it. I tried. You can't.
A rainbow came out under the village once. Under! I looked down on it. Walkers only ever see them from underneath, I suppose.
I want to fly up to the moon and knock on it. Gently. In case it's sleeping.
