The best sound a harp makes is the one just before it plays: the wind leaning on the strings, deciding. Hmm. There. Did you hear it decide?
A chord in Vell's tuning sounds like someone saying goodbye kindly. That's why the Evensong is in it. You can't sing the day down in a happy key; it won't go.
You know you've played well when the koi come to the edge of the pool. They like the middle strings. They don't care for my high notes at all. Critics, koi.
We keep a harp for each wind in the Hall, and one for no wind at all, that nobody plays. It's for still days. We hope never to hear it. Never trust a still day.
I can tell who's crossing the bridge by how the harps answer. Cirri make no sound at all. Walkers make the low strings shiver. You made them shiver.
Children always want to pluck the longest string first. Then they hear it and hide behind me. The long string sounds like a whale clearing its throat.
A harp's frame is skywood, and skywood remembers. Play one tune on it for years and it starts humming that tune by itself. Mine knows the Evensong by heart.
Every wind wants its own touch on the strings. Aure likes fingertips, Sefa the whole hand, Vell the thumb. Borre? Borre wants nobody touching anything.
work.harpist: Every wind wants its own tuning. Aure likes the strings slack and sweet; Borre wants them tight as a held breath.
Before the harps wake I hold up a wet finger, feel what {wind} is doing, and tell the pegs. They grumble. Pegs always grumble.
Walkers say a wind harp plays itself. It doesn't. It plays what you let it, and the letting is my whole trade.
Harp strings come up from the walkers as plain string. Three dawns soaked in dew and stretched across the Hall's rafters, and they've learned to sing.
The Hall of Echoes has seven echoes. On a still evening you can hear all seven answer, one after another, like a family calling each other home.
Leading the Evensong is mostly raising one hand at exactly the right moment and hoping the whole village is watching it.
Sefa is the hardest wind to play under. Warm and lazy: the strings sag, the notes slur, and the whole Hall sounds half asleep by noon.
Borre snapped four strings on me this morning. There's a red welt on my wrist from the last. Worth it: you should have heard the chord just before it went.
My first season as an apprentice, I was only allowed to dust the harps. I learned more from dusting than I ever did from playing.
Never tune in the noon sun. The frames swell, and by dusk you're a hair flat and the whole Evensong knows it.
The bell says dusk is one note. My harps say it's another. The village sings somewhere in between and calls it harmony.
A {job}'s fingertips go hard as skywood bark. Touch mine. Years of strings in there.
Some days the wind plays a phrase I've never heard, and I scramble to catch it before it blows on. Half our songs were stolen from the sky like that.
A cracked frame sings a little sour forever. We never throw one out. We give it to someone a bit sour themselves, with love, and it suits them.
Don't pluck a wind harp, {player}. Stroke it, the way you'd stroke a sleeping koi. Walkers always pluck.
The children fly into the Hall to shout their names and hear them come back seven times. I pretend to scold them. I did exactly the same.
A Cloud Whale passed close by the Hall once and sang. Every harp answered at once and nobody touched a string. I'll never play anything that good.
Before a storm the harps hum by themselves, low and nervous. I drape them in veilcloth, the way you'd cover a birdcage at night.
My teacher could tune by smell. "Peaches on the wind: that's Sefa, loosen the fourth string." Never wrong, not once.
The hardest part of leading the Evensong is stopping it. Everyone wants one more verse. The day's already down; let it rest.
Every harp in the Hall has a name. The great harp at the back of the stage is Old Gust. The little one by the door is Hiccup, and you'll know why the moment you pass it.
A sliver of amethyst set in a harp's bridge holds the tuning true for days. The skymerchant buys it off walkers for us, fair winds to them.
Sometimes I take a small harp down to the Cloud Garden and play for the koi. The gardeners say it settles them. I suspect the koi are being polite.
If you see me hovering by a harp with my eyes shut, I'm working. Truly. A harpist listens ten times for every note played.
The stage in the Hall is left open to the sky on purpose. The wind has to fly straight through, or the harps go dumb.
Vell is the harper's wind. A note on Vell carries clear across {village} and down through the clouds. Some nights I'm sure the bell-villages below can hear us.
My tuning pegs are skywood, turned from fallen branches. I've worn them smooth as peach stones.
Old harp strings never go to waste. The lamplighter twists them into wicks. I try not to think of my best notes burning.
My apprentice once tuned every harp to Borre on an Aure morning. The dawn sounded like two neighbours quarrelling. We still tease about it.
Truth be told, I can't hold a tune with my own voice. My hands do the singing for me.
When someone goes up past the blue, we play the Long Unwinding: every string loosened, one by one, until the harp falls quiet. It's the hardest piece we know.
Tune at dawn, play the morning in, mend strings by noon, teach the children, nap, lead the Evensong. The nap is the part I guard most fiercely.
The weavers say my harps are too loud for combing. I say their looms clack off the beat. We've agreed to disagree, loudly.
How does the wind know the tune? It doesn't. The wind brings the breath. We built the throat.
I've led more Evensongs than I can count, and my chest still flutters when the whole village comes in on the first note.
Wind a gold thread round the lowest string and it purrs. A trick from {village}'s first harpist. We don't share it with other villages. Well. Now I've shared it with you.
When a walker plays a wind harp, every Cirri near comes to listen. That isn't only politeness. We're checking your tuning.
A little tuning bar of gilded skystone hangs round my neck on a ribbon. Tap it on a knuckle and it gives the true note. I'd be lost without it.
There's a chord we only play at a Lengthening, as the new long veils unfurl. It makes even the bellkeeper cry.
After dark we play softly and leave the big harps covered. The old harpists said music draws phantoms, and nobody's brave enough to test it.
Borre alone on the harps, no hands at all, sounds like something old and grieving. I let it play. Some winds need to be heard out.
I don't play for praise. I play so the wind has somewhere to go. Praise is lovely, though. You may.
work.weaver: We fly up before Aure is properly awake, while the high wisps are still damp, and draw the cirrus out in long strands with our combs. Dry cloud tears. Dewy cloud stretches.
A veil comb has three hundred teeth of skywood, each split finer than a hair. My teacher's comb is older than the Loom House itself.
Spinning cloud is mostly patience. You roll it between finger and thumb until it remembers it would like to be a thread.
The blue at a veil's root isn't dye. It's the colour cirrus keeps when you take it from the very top of the sky. And the rose at the tips is dawn, caught in the fraying.
Gold runs down each edge of a veil. Not for show, whatever the skymerchant tells walkers. Gold keeps the edges from unravelling in Borre.
Most of my work is mending. A torn veil comes in, its owner trying hard not to cry, and I lay phantom membrane over the tear and stitch it down with string, small as I can.
Phantom membrane is the only patch that takes to cloud. Slice it thin, soak it overnight in rainwater, and it turns as clear as a moth's wing.
Weaving a child's long veils for the Lengthening takes a whole moon. I hum their name into every row. They never know. They fly straighter for it.
Veilcloth for awnings and cushions is easy: wide combs, loose weave, done by noon. Veils are another thing. One slipped thread and someone flies lopsided for a year.
The loom keeps a beat, clack and hush, clack and hush. My apprentice dozes off to it. So do I, some afternoons.
A walker once tied my best sky veilcloth round their shoulders and jumped off the Lift Dock to see if it would fly them. The windkeeper caught them, and my veilcloth, in that order.
The Cirrus Veil you walkers buy is a little cousin of ours: short, sturdy, forgiving. It won't fly you, but it will let you down gently.
Rose veilcloth takes longest. You may only comb the clouds that blush at sunrise, and they blush for about as long as it takes to say so.
My fingers are cold all year round. Cloud keeps the chill of the high air even indoors. Touch my hand if you don't believe me, {player}.
Fire stays out of the Loom House. Not a candle, not a lantern, not the lamplighter on a festival night. Especially not on a festival night.
There's a knot only weavers know, the Holdfast. Tie it right and the veil will tear before the knot gives. Tie it wrong and it slips in the first gust. No pressure.
Old veils are never thrown away. We unpick them and comb their cloud in with the new. Every veil in {village} has a little of someone's grandparent in it.
On a still day the cirrus droops and won't comb at all. "Never trust a still day." I'm certain a {job} said it first.
I can tell whose veils are whose from across the Veil Court, just by how they move. Who's tired, who's in love, who skipped breakfast. Veils tell everything.
My first veil had a pucker in it the size of a peach. My teacher flew on it for a whole year anyway, so I'd see that it could fly.
Children's veils are short so they can't fly too far. We let them out a hand's width every season, and the children measure each other constantly.
Never put a feather in a veil. Feathers belong in cushions. A veil with a feather woven in flies like a startled bird.
The best cirrus grows where a Cloud Whale has just swum through. The Old Singers comb the sky for us, in their way.
A gardener once begged a veilcloth net to shade the koi. I made it. By noon the koi had tangled themselves in it, all nine. We don't talk about it.
Every weaver has a mark, worked in near the root. Mine is three little stitches like a bird's foot. Look closely at the veils in {village}; you'll find it on half of them.
Sefa brings warm, loose cloud, good for cushions and little else. Borre's cloud is crisp as frost and makes the strongest veils in the sky, if your fingers survive the combing.
I mended a veil yesterday that had snagged on a skywood branch. Its owner swears the tree reached out for it. I sighed and said nothing about gardeners.
A loom for cloud is mostly empty space: a skywood frame, gold-wire heddles, and air. Cloud weaves best with room to breathe.
When I finish a pair of veils I hang them in the window for a night, so they can learn the wind before anyone flies on them.
Walkers buy veilcloth by the bolt and make carpets of it. Carpets. For walking on. I try very hard not to think about it.
The Loom House windows are always open, and weaving is quiet work. I hear every bit of gossip that floats past. I'm the best-informed Cirri in {village}, I'm told. Mostly by me.
My hands know the patterns so well I can weave and daydream together. Some of my best veils I don't remember making.
Never cut a veil-thread with a blade. Break it with your teeth, gently, like biting into a peach. Metal makes a veil remember the ground.
My apprentice has lovely hands and no patience whatsoever. I was the same. Patience grows. Hands don't.
A walker once asked me to mend their elytra. Stiff, strange wings. I patched them with membrane and string, and they flew. I hummed for a week.
The Lengthening is my favourite day and my most frightening. Every eye in the village is on the veils I made. If they flutter wrong, I'll feel it for a month.
Walkers' string comes in every thickness. I sort it by feel: fine for mending, middling for hems, thick for the harpists, who'd take it all if you let them.
Cloud gets tired. A veil worn every day for years needs fresh combing each spring, the way a cushion wants plumping.
How do I know a morning's good for combing? The dew sits on my eyelashes. If it doesn't, I go back to sleep.
"A Cirri is only as high as their veil is whole." Weavers hear it at every mending. It's flattering. It's also a great deal to carry.
I wove the rose hangings in the Veil Court. When the evening light comes through them the whole court goes pink, and I pretend not to watch people noticing.
Walkers' gold nuggets are beaten thin as breath and drawn through a pierced skystone to make veil-thread. My arms ache just telling you about it.
work.gardener: Grafting is the heart of the work. Slip a twig from a good old peach into a young skywood's bark, bind it with string, and wait. If the tree agrees, you'll have peaches by next spring.
The koi know my veils. When I fly over the pool they rise to meet me like little silver clouds. Anyone else, they scatter. I may be a touch smug about that.
Now and then a Cloud Koi sheds a Sky Scale. I find them floating at the pool's edge in the mornings and keep a pouch of them for whoever looks like they need luck.
A sky peach is ready when it smells like Sefa. Pick it a day early and it's hard as skystone; a day late and the bees have beaten you to it.
The garden's roots hang down through the bottom of the island. Once a moon I fly underneath to check them. It's dark and drippy under there, and I love it.
Peach blossom opens with Aure. If Borre takes the sky that week, I fly round wrapping every bud in veilcloth like a baby. Every one. Hundreds.
Every handful of soil in the Cloud Garden was carried up from far below by the first Cirri, a pouch at a time. We guard it like gold. Better than gold.
Koi are fussy eaters. Crumbs of peach, a pinch of pollen, a glow berry if they've been good. Never melon. They spit melon.
I count the koi every morning. Nine yesterday, nine today. One hides under the lily pads and I count it twice for luck.
Bees came up with the first gardeners, the story goes, in a hive lashed to someone's veils. Their great-great-grandchildren still work my peach trees.
Skywood leaves go gold at the edges when they're thirsty. I catch rain in veilcloth funnels and carry it round in a gourd, tree by tree.
Walkers think gardening is digging. I've never dug a thing in my life. I coax. There's a difference.
The weavers would like every cloud in the sky for combing. I need a few left alone to shade the koi at noon. We have a gentle arrangement, mostly made of glaring.
Any tree that grows too heavy at the island's edge gets pruned, however lovely. We all know what happened to the Belltowers.
Flowers in the Cloud Garden are chosen for the bees, the koi and the Evensong, in that order. Bluets for the bees, lilies of the valley for the dusk, pink tulips because the children ask.
Our saplings go down with walkers through the skymerchant. Somewhere below, a skywood is growing on the ground and wondering why it feels so heavy.
My hands smell of peach and pond water, always. There are worse things to smell of.
We split the bark for grafting with a sliver of amethyst, never a blade. It's cleaner, and the tree forgives it faster.
A koi went missing last spring. I found it three islets over, swimming happily round the Lantern Spire in the rain. They follow the wet.
Throwing peach stones off the edge is a crime in my garden. Somewhere down there a walker takes one on the head. I once heard the yelp all the way up.
The children help with the peach harvest. One for the basket, one for the mouth. I've learned to plan for half.
Koi sleep with their eyes open. My first season as a {job} I thought they were all ill, and sat up three nights singing to them.
Glow berries grow on the undersides of the islands, among the hanging roots. I pick them upside down. It is not dignified.
When an old skywood dies, we never burn it. We let it break down slowly and the garden drinks it back. The harpists get the best branches for pegs.
A Cloud Koi outlives any of us. The oldest in our pool was here when my teacher's teacher was learning. It looks at me like I'm new.
I plant peach stones along the islet edges. Their roots hold the soil when Borre comes looking to take it.
Every dawn bell, every dusk bell, every storm peal: the koi dive. I've asked for a softer bell. I was told the bell is the bell.
In a good peach year you can smell {village} from three islets off. Walkers come up the Wind Stone just following their noses.
I'm grafting a tree with three peaches on one trunk: gold, rose, and a little white one nobody's named. Taste one when they ripen and I'll name it after you, {player}.
Moss on the pool stones keeps the water sweet. Scrape it off and the koi go pale and sullen. Leave it, and they shine.
Seeds blow up from the ground on Sefa's warm breath and land in my beds: thistle, dandelion, once a whole pumpkin vine. I pull them gently and send them home.
Rot in a peach tree spreads like a rumour. One brown spot at dawn, a whole branch by the Evensong. So I check the bark every single morning.
Stand on the bridge, not over the koi pool, if you don't mind. It isn't you. It's your feet. They've never seen feet.
The trees all have names. The crooked old one by the pool is Patience. The young one that drops its fruit early is Fidget.
Half of gardening up here is gardening. The other half is stopping it all blowing away. I've pinned whole flowerbeds down with skywood pegs before a Borre night.
Walkers ask if peaches grow on the ground too. They do, I tell them. Very slowly. And very heavily.
Sky Scales come off when the koi are happy, I tell the children. Maybe they come off when the koi are itchy. Either way, they're lucky.
Pollen gets everywhere in spring: my hair, my veils, the creases of my eyelids. I sneeze gold for a month.
The best hour in the garden is just after the Evensong. The koi glimmer, the peach leaves whisper, and nobody needs a thing from me.
My apprentice once planted a sapling upside down. It grew anyway, crooked and stubborn, and it's the best tree in the garden now.
Every morning I skim the pool with a veilcloth net to clear the fallen leaves. The koi try to swim into it. I'm fairly sure it's a game.
Some walkers ask if the koi are for eating. I simply hover there and let the silence answer.
work.bellkeeper: The bell rope is braided from forty strands of walkers' string and three of gold. It's longer than me with my veils out, and my hands know every knot in it.
Dawn bell, dusk bell, storm peal. Three songs, that's all I play. The harpists find this hilarious. The village gets up all the same.
Ringing at dawn means waking before dawn, and that means sleeping before the Evensong ends. I've never once heard its last verse.
Our bell is as thin as we could make it and as light as we dared. The old belltowers hung iron bells as heavy as whales, and you know where those villages are now.
A storm peal is long and uneven on purpose: ring, ring, pause, ring. It's not music. It's a warning, and everyone in {village} knows it in their bones.
All day I watch for storms. Borre sharpens, the high wisps vanish, the koi dive early and the chimes go quiet. When all four happen, I ring.
Ring the storm peal too early and they'll call you a worrier. Ring it too late and someone's caught over the edge in lightning. I'd rather be called a worrier.
Every dawn gets a notch in the beam above the bell. This world has seen {day} dawns. I've rung in a fair few of them myself.
The pagoda has three roofs and a chime under every eave. When all of them ring at once, the wind can't make up its mind.
I've the strongest arms in {village}. Ask anyone. Actually, don't ask the weavers.
Children sneak up the pagoda to touch the bell. I let them: one finger, very gently, and they feel the hum all the way to their elbows. Their faces!
Dusk is the harder bell. You ring it gently, so the day knows it may go. Dawn you ring bright: up, up, the sky is waiting.
Never ring the bell for fun. I did once, as an apprentice, and the whole village flew out to the Veil Court still sleep-curled, sure a storm was coming.
Bell first, then lanterns: that's the dusk rule. The lamplighter has been early twice this moon. I have noticed.
Every fifth dawn I polish the bell with a pad of veilcloth and a dab of beeswax. It keeps the note sweet. Please don't lick it.
A bell's voice changes with the weather. In snow it rings higher and thinner; on Sefa's warm days it goes round and lazy. I change my pull to match.
I'm told the bell-villages below let anyone pull their bells. Anyone! Up here only the {job} touches the rope.
Keeping time is more than ringing. Is it noon yet? How many dawns to the Lengthening? When did the last whale pass? I'm the village's memory, with a rope attached.
When someone goes up past the blue, the bell rings once, softly, at noon, and then not again till dusk. That silence is the loudest thing I do all year.
A thread of gold runs across the pagoda floor. When the bell's shadow lies on it, it's noon, and I give a little tap for anyone listening.
They say the rope chooses the next bellkeeper. It chose me by catching round my ankle when I was small and swinging me clear across the pagoda.
There's only ever one bellkeeper. It's a little lonely. No one else wakes in the dark listening for the hour.
A good dawn bell sets the koi rising, the harps humming and the peach blossoms opening. Or so I like to think. The gardeners say the blossoms manage on their own.
I dropped the clapper off the edge once while I was oiling it. It's somewhere on the ground. I like to think a walker found it and is still wondering.
There's a crack in the bell, hair-thin, near the lip. Older than me. It gives the dusk bell a little catch, like someone about to cry. I wouldn't mend it for anything.
The most I've ever rung: three storm peals in three nights. My palms were raw for a week. Nobody was caught out. I'd do it again tomorrow.
Before you ask, {player}: no, you may not ring it. Yes, I know you'd do it gently. Everyone says that.
My favourite moment is the breath before the dawn bell. Everything still, all {village} asleep, and I'm holding the morning in my hands.
Cloud Whales answer the bell sometimes. One long, low note from very far off, just after dusk. I hold the rope still and listen until it's done.
When the bell is quiet I rest my forehead on it and hum. It hums back. We're not strange, bellkeepers. We just listen to something you can't hear.
Does the noise bother me? The bell isn't noise. Noise is a walker in iron boots coming up onto the Lift Dock.
My apprentice once rang the dusk bell in the middle of the Evensong, sure they were late. The whole village stopped singing and stared. They've never been early since.
When a baby is born, the next dawn bell has three quick little rings before it. Listen for them. It's the happiest sound in the sky.
The bell has to reach every nest, even on the far islets. I swing it toward the rim at dawn and toward the court at dusk. People swear they can hear the difference.
My knees ache before a storm, and I've never knelt on anything in my life. The bell knows, my knees know, and then Borre arrives.
Fireworks are my nightmare. A walker sets one off below, every Cirri thinks it's thunder, and every face turns to me. I had to invent an all-clear peal on the spot.
I sleep in the open top tier, curled over a cushion right under the bell. If it so much as shivers in the night, I'm awake.
Storms belong to me and the windkeeper both. I ring the peal; they fetch every walker in off the Lift Dock. We've never lost one.
Every storm gets a knot in a long cord I keep: a big knot for thunder, a small one for rain, a bead for snow. The cord's three veils long now.
The dawn bell has never once been late in my time. On the morning it is, come and check on me.
People think my work is pulling a rope. It's mostly waiting: watching the light, feeling the wind, holding still for exactly the right moment. The pull is the easy bit.
You ring from the shoulders, never the wrists, or your arms are ruined by spring. I teach the children with a peach on a string.
work.lamplighter: I'm the only one in {village} who carries fire. Caged in gold, always, never once loose. People still fly a little wide of me at dusk. I don't mind.
My pole is skywood, three times my own length, with a gold hook at one end and a snuffing cup at the other. I could find either in the dark. I usually do.
Wick-trimming is the real craft. Too long and the flame climbs and blackens the gold. Too short and it drowns in its own wax. I trim each one to a fingernail.
The great lantern is a cluster of cages under the spire's gilded cap, with one more on the very point. Lighting them all takes exactly the Evensong's first verse.
From the top of the Lantern Spire at dusk I can see the bell-villages' lights coming on far below, little sparks in the dark. I always wave. Nobody ever waves back.
Afraid of fire? Of course I am. Every Cirri is. That's what makes me good at this. A lamplighter who isn't afraid is a lamplighter who gets careless.
Our wax comes from the gardeners' bees and our wicks from old harp strings. So every light in {village} is a little bit garden and a little bit song.
A skin of rainwater on my belt, a wet veilcloth over one shoulder. I haven't needed either in years. I'll never go a night without them.
The weavers won't let me past the Loom House door after dusk, not even with the lantern shuttered. I support this entirely.
At dawn I fly the bridges and snuff every lantern with the cup on my pole. Click, click, click. It's the quietest work in the village, and the loveliest.
Walkers cross our bridges by lantern light and never look up. If they did, they'd see me hovering under the rail with my pole, fixing their light.
A lantern that gutters is telling me something: a draught from the wrong side, the wax gone soft, a moth in the cage. It's usually the moth.
Phantoms hate the great lantern. They circle out past its light and won't come closer. That's why it burns all night, every night.
The gold on a cage has to be polished every few dawns, or the light goes yellow and sad. A scrap of veilcloth and a great deal of breath.
I make the sky lanterns the skymerchant sells you walkers: gold nuggets bent into a cage round a little flame. Keep it away from anything dry, please.
My hands smell of wax and smoke. The children wrinkle their noses at me, then beg to see the flame. Every time, both.
I set my own hem alight once, as an apprentice. I put it out in the koi pool. The koi have never forgiven me.
The bellkeeper insists my lanterns have been early. My lanterns have not been early. My lanterns have been prompt.
Lighting the great lantern in a strong Vell is like threading a needle in a sneeze. You shield the taper with your whole body and both veils, and you hold your breath.
A lamplighter's veils go singed at the tips. Look at mine: little brown freckles. The weavers keep offering to mend them. I like them. They're my years.
Every bridge in {village} has its lanterns spaced so a walker is never more than four steps from light. I paced it out myself, flying, with my feet pretending.
On the longest night of the year we light every lantern in the village together, and the whole island glows like a peach held up to the sun.
They say you can see our great lantern from the next village on a clear night. Some nights I swear theirs blinks back. Lamplighters keep each other company like that.
Nobody cooks. I know that. But I once held a peach over a lantern to see what would happen. It went brown and smelled wonderful and I felt terribly guilty.
Snuffing is better than blowing. Blow a lantern out and the smoke goes everywhere. Snuff it and it just sighs and stops, like a child falling asleep.
My apprentice isn't allowed the taper yet. They carry the wax, the wicks, the snuffer. Maybe next spring. Fire can wait for a steady hand.
A cracked pane is the worst thing I can find on my rounds. Wind gets in, the flame leans, the gold heats. I carry spare panes in a pouch and fit them with shaking fingers.
Most Cirri fear fire loudly. Mine is a quiet fear, more like respect. Fire is a guest you never turn your back on.
Lantern light makes the koi glow on the bottom of the pool. The gardeners say it unsettles them. I say they're showing off.
Why not glow berries in every cage? I tried. A cage of glow berries is pretty and faint, and walkers fall off bridges in faint.
There's a ladder inside the Lantern Spire, just for walkers. I've never used it, but I keep it polished. Want to come up and watch the great lantern lit, {player}?
I measure the night in candle-stubs. Tall at dusk, a stub by dawn. When I change them I know to a breath how long the dark has been.
The lantern stage wears a crust of old wax a hand thick, like old snow. Every spring I scrape it off and roll it into new candles between my palms.
When someone goes up past the blue, I leave the lantern by their nest unlit for one night. The dark gap in the lights says it better than words.
Fireworks? I'd ground anyone who brought one near my lanterns. Well. I'd want to.
Court first, then the near bridges, then the islets one by one, and the great lantern last as the Evensong rises. I could do the rounds with my eyes shut. I don't.
When the wind's wrong I light the great lantern from right in among the cages, curled under the gilded cap like a moth. Don't tell the weavers I fit.
Walkers carry torches! Raw flame on a stick, no cage at all, waved about like nothing. I want to scold them, and also ask how they're so brave.
A good {job} is never noticed. If nobody remembers the lanterns, they were lit right.
I love the moment the great lantern catches. One cage, then the next, then the whole cluster, and the gold throws light on every veil in the Veil Court. Everyone looks up, just for a breath.
Glowing candles stand in the nest windows too. I trim them for the old ones who can't fly the rounds any more, and they pay me in honey and stories.
Wicks are twisted from three strands: one for dusk, one for midnight, one for dawn, my teacher said. It isn't true. I still say it while I twist.
work.skymerchant: Phantom membrane is the dearest thing a walker can bring me. It's the only patch that takes to a torn veil. Every membrane you sell me keeps a Cirri flying.
Feet planted, that's how walkers haggle. I haggle drifting slowly backwards. It works wonders. They always follow.
Fresh stock every dawn: peaches from the garden, veilcloth from the Loom House, lanterns from the spire. By noon the best of it has gone down with the early walkers.
Feathers go into nest cushions. A good cushion takes a hundred. We sleep curled in the air above them, so they must be soft enough to dream on.
Amethyst goes to the harpists and the chime-makers. It rings true. A chime with a sliver of amethyst in it sings in the faintest breath.
Truth be told, we've little use for emeralds up here. They're green and heavy, a little piece of the ground. But walkers trust them, so I keep a jar.
The Windsong Flute is my favourite sale. Play it near any Cirri and they'll stop whatever they're doing to listen. Even me. Especially me.
A walker once tried to buy the Wind Stone. The actual stone. I offered the Lift Dock and the windkeeper as well, and watched them slowly work out I was teasing.
Wind harps don't fit in walkers' pockets, I've learned. They try. Oh, how they try.
Down below, I'm told, walkers build whole walls of skystone bricks. So heavy you'd think they wanted to sink. Well, they're on the ground already. Nowhere further to sink.
The weavers think I sell their veilcloth too cheap. I think they'd rather keep it all and sleep in it. We're both a little right.
I can spot a walker's first visit by how they stand: arms out, knees bent, staring at the gaps between the planks. I always offer them a peach first.
Haggling is a dance. You name a price, they name a smaller one, you both sigh, you both look at the clouds, and then somebody laughs. It's all in the laugh.
A Cirrus Veil lets you down gently. It does not take you up. I tell every walker who buys one, and every one of them tries jumping upward anyway.
Cloud blocks go faster than the weavers can spare them. Walkers stack them up in their gardens below. Imagine. Cloud, on the ground, sitting still.
String! Walkers bring it by the armful and I can never get enough. Harp strings, veil mending, bell rope, lantern wicks. All of {village} is tied together with walkers' string.
When a walker buys a sapling, I make them promise to plant it somewhere high. Next time they come up, I ask after the tree.
Gilded skystone is our finest stone. Walkers buy it by the block to make their houses look as if the dawn landed on them.
My stall has three rules: no fire in the pavilion, no fireworks anywhere, no haggling before you've said fair wind. The last one is the strictest.
A walker came up once with a stack of phantom membranes taller than they were. I looped twice, paid double, and flew straight to the Loom House with them.
Earth, smoke, iron: walkers smell of the ground. I've come to like it. It smells like somewhere very far away.
The Market Pavilion looks straight at the Lift Dock. I see every walker before they see me, and I've a peach in hand by the time they reach the top.
The windkeeper says they greet walkers first. I say I greet them better. The walkers say we both talk too much.
Wind chimes sell best of all. Walkers hang them on their houses and swear the wind sounds different after. It doesn't. They've just started listening.
A good {job} knows what a thing's worth to both sides. A peach is nothing much to a walker and a whole morning's care to a gardener. I never sell what I can't explain.
Children love to help at the stall. They hide in the veilcloth and leap out at walkers. I've lost two good customers that way and gained a dozen stories.
You'd not believe what walkers try to pay with. Once, a single boot. I asked what we'd do with one boot. They said they'd hoped I would know.
Restocking means flying the rounds before the market opens: garden, Loom House, spire, Hall of Echoes. Everyone hands me their best and begs me not to sell it cheap.
My secret for trade? Smile, be honest, and know where the nearest edge is. Some walkers back away from a good price and forget there's nothing behind them.
I've never been to the ground, but I've traded with so many walkers I could tell you whose fields grow the fattest carrots and whose roads are muddiest.
Now and then the walkers who borrowed wings come by, all swagger, elytra folded. I sell them membrane for their patches and pretend I'm not impressed.
Feathers, amethyst, membrane, string. Bring me any of the four and you'll never leave my stall empty-handed.
A good trade leaves both sides flying high. If one of us is low after, it wasn't a trade. It was a theft with manners.
Up here we price things by how light they are. A feather is worth a great deal. A brick is worth very little. Walkers find this baffling, and excellent value on bricks.
Every dawn I count the stock, every dusk I count the emeralds, and in between I count the walkers. Counting is half of trade. Smiling is the other half.
Gossip comes free with every purchase. Walkers tell me the news below; I carry it to the Evensong. I'm the nearest thing {village} has to a window on the ground.
Walkers eat their peaches right at the stall, standing up, juice down to their wrists. Nothing has ever looked so cheerful. I nearly gave the next one away.
Trade goes slow when Borre has the sky. Walkers don't love the Lift Dock with a cold wind trying to push them off it.
I keep a shelf of things walkers have left behind: a map, a compass that spins, a book in a hand I can't read. Someday someone will come back for them.
The skymerchant before me could sell a cloud to a cloud. I'm still learning. I can sell a cloud to a walker, which is easier.
Ground comes up on walkers' boots and settles all over the pavilion. Every evening I sweep the dust off the edge. Gently. It's only going home.
Here's a secret: I haggle hardest over membrane and softest over string. Don't tell the walkers. Oh. You're a walker. Well, now you know.
work.windkeeper: The Wind Stone stands far below in its ring of skystone. I've never touched it. Once a moon I fly down until I'm just above it, listen to it hum, and come home quick.
The column has a voice. A true column hums low, like a whale a long way off. A thin one whistles. When it whistles, I go down and look.
My first task every morning: drop a feather into the shaft and watch it come back up. If it comes back, the column's sound. If it doesn't, my day has started early.
Walkers come up the column with their arms flailing, nearly all of them. I hover at the landing and catch an elbow just as they reach the dock. Some of them hug me.
The Courtesy is the oldest promise we have. The first windkeepers set the stones so walkers could visit, and I keep the promise. That's the whole job. The rest is detail.
A sheep wandered into the ring once and rode the wind all the way up, bleating. We kept it a week. The children named it Cloud and cried when it went down.
Reading the winds: wet a finger, watch the wisps below, listen to the dock chimes. Today it's {wind}, and I knew it before the dawn bell.
Going down is the hard part for walkers. Step into the shaft, hold yourself small, and the wind lets you down like a hand lowering a peach. Most of them shut their eyes.
Those rails on the dock went up for walkers, the year one leaned out to admire the view and just kept leaning.
I'm awake before anyone comes up and after the last one goes down. Some nights a walker turns up at midnight and finds me there with a lantern, yawning.
Iron is the worst thing to carry up. Armour, anvils, a minecart once. Heavy things make the column groan. The Courtesy is for everyone, so I don't stop them. But I wince.
Borre pushes the column sideways. On Borre days I fly alongside walkers on the way up and nudge them back to the middle. They think I'm being friendly. I am. Also.
Every walker who comes up hears "fair wind" from me first. Even the rude ones. Especially the rude ones. It's hard to stay rude when someone's glad you came.
I remember every walker who's come up: faces, names, what they carried. I'm the first friend {village} gives them, and I take that seriously.
Old windkeepers could hear a walker step into the ring from up here, they say. I can't. I like to think the stones are quieter now, and not that I'm going deaf.
Phantoms try the column at night, riding it up like a road. I chase them off with a lantern. We need their membrane, but not delivered like that.
Anyone with borrowed wings skips the column entirely. They swoop in over the rail and land all wrong. I tell them about the Wind Stone anyway. Manners.
I teach the children to read the wind from the dock: toss a petal, watch it go, name the wind. They always guess Sefa, because Sefa smells of peaches and they're always hungry.
Every gust coming up the column tugs at my veils. I've got tangles in mine the weavers despair of.
When a walker reaches the dock pale and shaking, I don't talk. I just hover beside them and point out the view until their knees stop trembling.
Each wind lifts differently. Aure gently. Vell singing. Sefa lazily, and it might stop for a nap halfway. Borre like it's throwing you.
Snow in the column is the prettiest thing I know. Flakes falling, flakes rising, and a walker in the middle of it all going up with their mouth open.
My teacher called the Wind Stone a door with no walls. Keep it open, keep it kind, and never let a walker hold sneak halfway up by mistake.
A calm walker comes up in about eleven breaths. A frightened one, about eleven shrieks.
Down round the stone, walkers leave things: a flower in the ring, a name scratched in the dirt, a bowl of berries. I think they're thanking it. I think it knows.
Open sky on three sides: the Lift Dock is the very edge of {village}. People ask how I can stand it. I'm a Cirri. Edges are where the sky begins.
The skymerchant has a peach waiting for every walker I bring up. I've stopped minding. A walker with a peach is a happy walker, and a happy walker comes back.
If the column ever failed, a walker halfway up would fall. So I check it at dawn, noon and dusk, and I sleep with one ear toward the shaft.
Chimes hang round the dock, each tuned to a different wind. When the right one rings, I know who's coming before the clouds do.
In my time I've caught a hat, a cake and one very confused chicken coming up the column. Most things that go up come down again. Not on my watch.
How does a walker get down? Same way they came up, I tell them, only backwards and calmer.
My wrists prickle an hour before Borre comes. My teacher's prickled a whole day ahead. It's the one part of the trade nobody can teach you.
Some walkers come up once, look round, and go straight back down. That's all right. The sky is a lot. I hope they dream about it.
I'm the first face anyone sees up here, so I comb my veils before every visitor. I try to. The column has other ideas.
Every dusk I fly a slow circle round the shaft and sing the column a little of the Evensong. Nobody told me to. It just seems rude to leave it out.
No one remembers how the stones were set. Every {job} has a theory. Mine is that the first ones asked the Old Singers, and the whales sang the wind into the ground.
A stone with no keeper goes lazy. The column thins, the hum drops, the walkers stop coming. Ours won't go lazy. Not while I've breath.
Pets come up too. Dogs go up barking and arrive silent. Cats go up silent and arrive furious.
On busy days I've had three walkers in the column at once, stacked like peaches in a basket. I talk to each of them the whole way. Mostly I say "nearly there".
Halfway up their first time, one walker this spring stopped screaming and started laughing. That's when I knew they'd be back.
Rain pours past the dock into the shaft and comes back up as mist. Some mornings the column looks like a waterfall running the wrong way.
Walkers think I'm a guard. I'm not. I'm a host. A guard keeps people out. I'm here so you can come in, {player}.
work.none: No trade of my own. Today I've carried cloud for the weavers, held the lamplighter's pole and been splashed by three separate koi. A good day.
What do I do? Whatever the wind needs. This morning that was chasing a runaway cushion across three islets.
Every trade in {village} has called on me at least once. I can almost tune a harp, almost mend a veil and almost ring the bell. Almost is very useful.
I never settled on one trade. My threads wandered at the loom, and the koi liked me too much to let me work. So now I go wherever I'm wanted.
When the gardeners shake the peach trees, someone has to swoop about underneath with a basket. That's me. I only miss a few, and some walker down there has a lucky day.
I mind the little ones while their parents work. Mostly I mind them loudly, because they're upside down in a skywood tree.
When a walker gets lost on the bridges, I'm usually the one who finds them. I've no dock or stall to keep. I have time, and time is good for finding people.
People think no trade means nothing to do. I've never been busier in my life. Everyone needs a hand, and they all pay in peaches.
Before a storm I fly the rim and call everyone in. Nobody asked me to. Somebody had to. Now it's mine.
My work is the space between everyone else's work. Carrying, fetching, holding, helping. I'm the string that ties the village together. Oh, I like that. I'll say it again.
Some days the wind needs nothing from me, and I spend the afternoon drifting over the edge, keeping the clouds company. Someone has to.
I used to feel low, having no trade. Then a weaver told me a veil isn't only its gold thread; it's mostly the cloud in between. That helped.
I sing the low part in the Evensong. That's my one sure job. Everything else depends on the day.
A koi got out of the pool this morning and I chased it twice round the Bell Pagoda. The gardener was busy. The koi was fast. I was faster, in the end.
Who sweeps the walkers' dust off the bridges? Me. Who untangles the wind chimes after Borre? Me. Who's told me to stop being so modest? Nobody, yet.
I carry messages, nest to nest, islet to islet. You'd be amazed what people would rather say across a bridge than to a face.
Before a Lengthening the weavers need extra hands for combing, and I'm up before Aure for a week. Nobody combs faster than someone with nothing better to do.
I hold things. The far end of a bolt of veilcloth. A harp steady while it's tuned. A nervous walker's hand at the top of the Lift Dock.
My grandparents were bellkeepers and my parents were gardeners. I was meant to be something. I became a little of everything.
There's no trade for me to pass on, so I've no apprentice. The children follow me round anyway. I think they're learning to be useful. Or to be late.
The wind sends me where I'm needed. Today it sent me to the Loom House, then the Cloud Garden, then home for a nap. The wind is very wise.
When a trade's short of hands, I step in. I rang the dusk bell once when the bellkeeper had a cold. Only half a beat late. I'm still very proud of it.
You walkers must have a word for someone who does every job. We just say "the wind's hands". I'm one of those.
If you need anything while you're up here, {player}, ask me. I'm always busy, but I'm never too busy. That's the whole trick of it.
After the Evensong I tidy the Veil Court: fallen petals, lost ribbons, a child asleep in the air. I carry them home one at a time. The children, I mean. The petals stay.
work.on: Talk to me while I work, I don't mind. Hands busy, ears free.
One moment... there. Sorry, you caught me in the middle of something fiddly. Go on.
Mind where you put your feet, walker. Everything here is either delicate or sharp, or both.
Stay and watch if you like. Everyone thinks it looks easy. Everyone.
You've found me at my spot, so I'll be talking with my back half turned. Don't take it to heart.
A visitor at work! Nobody visits at work. Except the children, and they don't count; they borrow things and never bring them back.
I can talk and work at once. I can't talk, work and answer questions about my work at once. Pick two.
Hold this for me? No, the other end. There. You're a natural.
You've come at a good time. The wind's steady and the work's going well. Don't say it out loud.
Give me a light breeze to finish this bit, then I'm all yours.
Watch my hands, not my face. My face is concentrating, and it looks fiercer than I mean it to.
If I stop answering, it isn't rudeness. The work has taken the rest of me. Poke me gently.
Everyone in {village} comes past my spot at least once a day. You're the first walker this week, though.
Shh, just a breath... Lovely. Right. Where were we?
Can't stop, but I can chat. Come round this side, the light's better.
People say I hum while I work. I don't believe them. I'd notice. Wouldn't I?
At it since the dawn bell. Arms tired, heart high. That's the right way round.
Careful, {player}, you're exactly where I need to be in about three breaths. There. Thank you.
Ask me anything. I've been working alone for hours and talking to myself has grown dull.
Working with a walker watching makes me nervous. Good nervous. I'll do it beautifully, you'll see.
work.off: No, I'm not working. My work's over there, missing me. Let it miss me a while.
Ask me about my work tomorrow. Today I'm just a Cirri on a breeze.
Even the wind rests between gusts. That's where you've found me.
You've caught me playing truant. Don't tell anyone. Well. Everyone knows already.
The work will still be there when I get back. It's very loyal like that.
Away from my spot I forget I've got a trade at all. It's lovely. Then I see something that needs doing, and I remember.
My hands keep making the motions even when I'm off. Look, they're doing it now. I can't stop them.
I'm taking a light breeze. A long light breeze. A light gale, really.
Work? I'm out here admiring the clouds below. That's work too, if you do it properly.
Don't let me look at my spot. If I look at it, I'll go back. Talk to me instead. Good.
I came out to stretch my veils. Nobody works well with crumpled veils.
I left my work in good hands. Mine. They'll be back soon.
I should be glad to be away, and I am. But I keep wondering if I left something half-done. I always have.
Nobody needs me for a whole hour. Isn't that strange? I keep looking round for someone to help.
My teacher said resting is part of the work. I'm being very thorough with that part today.
Catch me at my spot if you want to talk shop. Out here I only talk wind and gossip.
Out on the breeze I get my best ideas for work. By the time I'm back, I've forgotten them. A cruel arrangement.
I flew a loop round the whole village before I could stop myself. Work makes you stiff. Looping fixes it.
If anyone asks, I'm out here checking the wind for the work. Very professionally. Very important.
Not on duty, not in a hurry, not wishing I were anywhere else. Fair wind, walker. It's a rare hour.
work.weather.rain: Rain on the awnings, rain on the bridges, rain falling on past us into the clouds below. Work goes on. It just goes on damp.
Wet veils are heavy veils. On rain days we work slowly and keep low over the islands, and nobody minds.
The gardeners are glad, the weavers are grumbling, and the lamplighter's checking every pane twice. That's a rain day for you.
Cold, slippery hands, and everything takes twice as long. Still, I'd rather work in the rain than sit and listen to it.
Rain is good for one thing at work: nobody comes by to chat. Except you. Which is nice, actually.
My tools are hung under the eaves to drip, and the rain plinks off them like a little harp. Better company than some.
We say rain is the clouds going down to visit their cousins. It makes the work slow, but you can't hurry a visit.
The walkers below need this rain more than we do. I remind myself of that every time a drop runs down my collar.
Half the village has come indoors to work, so wherever you turn there's someone at your elbow. Cosy. Crowded. Both.
In rain, every finished thing has to be wrapped in veilcloth and stowed dry. I spend more of the day wrapping than working.
work.weather.thunder: No work in thunder. Tools down, everyone home, the children in the middle of the nest. The work will forgive us.
When Borre throws lightning, nothing in {village} matters but getting everyone under a roof. Not the harps, not the peaches. People.
I left everything half-done when the storm peal rang. My heart's still pounding. Work can wait. Hearts can't.
A storm turns every trade into one trade: counting heads. Is everyone in? Is everyone in? Then we hum.
Thunder rolls up through the whole island and into your chest. I couldn't hold anything steady in this if I tried.
The bell has rung, the lanterns are shuttered, the koi have gone deep. Nothing left to do but wait it out.
Every Cirri drops their work for thunder. Even the proud ones. Especially the proud ones; they just pretend they meant to stop.
Why are you out in this, {player}? Come under the eaves. Your work can wait as well as mine.
Lightning loves anything that sticks up: harp frames, the lantern's gold cap, the pagoda's point. We keep well clear of all of it till the storm moves on.
Tomorrow will be all mending: torn awnings, scattered blossom, a chime blown off its hook. Today we hide. That's a storm day's work.
work.weather.snow: Up here the snow is born right beside us. You can watch the first flakes form before they fall. Hard to keep your mind on work with that to look at.
Cold fingers make clumsy work. I blow on mine and carry on. Snow days are slow days.
Snow settles on every awning and bridge rail, and someone has to brush it off before the weight builds. Heavy is dangerous, even when it's pretty.
In snow everything goes quiet, even the work. Between tasks I can hear my own breath.
The children are no help at all today; all they want is to catch flakes on their tongues. I've caught three myself. Don't tell.
Snow means short days and long nights, and the work has to fit in between. I start before the bell and finish in the dark.
A Borre snow bites. A Vell snow drifts. You can work through the drifting kind, if you keep your hands moving.
Everything I make on a snow day comes out a little crisper, standing a little straighter. Something in the cold gets into it.
Snow on the veils! Shake, shake. Let it sit and it melts into the weave, and then you're flying damp all afternoon.
On snow days half the village works in veilcloth mittens. Terrible for fine work. Wonderful for everything else.
time.dawn: The weavers are already out with their combs, raking in cirrus while it's still damp enough to hold a thread.
Did the dawn bell wake you? It always rings just as I've found the soft side of my cushion.
At this hour the tips of my veils are the same rose as the sky. For a breath I can't tell where I stop and the morning starts.
Look down. The cloud sea is pink from edge to edge, and not one walker under it knows.
I shook the dew off my veils over the Cloud Garden and made a little rain of my own. The flowers looked so surprised.
First light finds the gilded roofs before it finds anyone's face. For a moment the whole village blinks gold.
This sky has seen {day} dawns now, and I'd swear no two of them were the same colour.
Every dawn I eat a peach hanging upside down over the garden. Don't ask why. It tastes better that way.
The bell rings, the koi stir, the harps catch the first breath of wind. Same order every dawn. I'd be lost if it ever changed.
The night-moths are sinking away into the cloud. I always feel the whole village breathe out when the last one goes.
Listen: everyone's shaking the dew out of their veils. A hundred little snaps all over the village, like the sky cracking its knuckles.
Nobody says much before the bell. We just hover and watch the light come, all of us facing east like flowers.
Dawn's the only hour I can see the bell-villages far below, their chimney smoke standing straight up like threads.
The children always try to catch the first sunbeam. They never manage it, but they come back glowing anyway.
You're up with the bell, {player}! I thought walkers slept until the sun came and kicked them.
time.morning: Mornings are for work and gossip, in that order. Well. Usually in that order.
Up go the awnings on the Market Pavilion. By the time they're tied, a walker always comes puffing up from the Lift Dock.
The harpists are tuning to {wind} now. Every string has to learn the day's wind fresh, they say, or it sings flat until dusk.
So bright, the cloud sea at this hour. I fly with my eyes half shut. Walkers squint at snow; we squint at the floor.
I've already had two peaches and a quarrel with a bee. It's been a full morning.
Flying lessons over the Veil Court this morning. Lots of shrieking. Some of it from the teachers.
The koi know it's morning. They crowd round the gardeners in a gold-and-white tangle, begging like children.
The islands' shadows lie across the clouds below like dark boats. By noon they'll have shrunk to nothing.
Dawn veils are heavy with dew. Morning veils are light as gossip. Now's the time to fly anywhere you like.
A good morning is one where nothing needs mending. Today might be one. Ask me again at noon.
What do walkers do first thing in the morning? I picture a great deal of stamping about.
Guests can manage the bridges now they're dry. At dawn the planks are slick with dew and walkers go over them like cats on ice.
The weavers have hung last night's veilcloth out to air. The whole Loom House flutters like it wants to come flying too.
Swallows went by underneath me just now, hunting over the cloud sea. I always want to wave, but they never look up.
{player}, you look rested. Walkers sleep lying flat, don't you? On purpose? It sounds like falling and never landing.
time.noon: Noon, and the sun's right on top of us. The only shade in the whole village is underneath it.
At midday half of us hang in the shadow under the islands, among the roots, like bats with better manners.
The calcite's so bright at noon it hurts. I keep my eyes on my own veils and fly from memory.
Touch the bridge rail. Go on. Warm as a peach in the sun, isn't it?
The koi have all drifted into the shade under the skywood trees, and they won't come out until it moves round.
A peach picked at noon is warm right through. I had one with honey and now I can't think about anything else.
Heat comes up off the islands in shimmers. Look through it and the far islets wobble like they're laughing at something.
Midday's a lazy hour. Even the harps go quiet, as if the wind had gone for a nap.
Walkers were crossing the bridge just now, red as apples, fanning themselves with their hats. I wanted to fan them with my veils.
The sun's so high my shadow drops straight down through the cloud. Somewhere on the ground there's a dark patch shaped like me, and I'll never meet it.
Noon is for honey and dozing, in the air over the Cloud Garden where the leaves throw a little shade.
The bridge planks tick as they warm. Guests always think something's about to give way. Nothing ever does. Nearly never.
I dipped down into the cloud to get out of the glare, and came back up wet as a sponge. Not worth it.
Half the day gone, and I've done exactly half of what I meant to. That's honest, at least.
{player}! Out in the noon sun with no hat and no veil? Walkers are braver than they are sensible.
time.afternoon: Afternoons are long up here. The sun takes its time going west, and so do we.
The harpists have started practising for the Evensong already. You can hear the same three bars from every bridge.
The light's gone honey-coloured. Everyone looks kinder in it, even walkers.
This is the hour the children get bored and race round the Lantern Spire. Three laps and back, and somebody always cuts the corner.
The cloud sea heaps itself up into towers in the afternoon heat. From here they look like a second village nobody lives in.
Most walkers come up in the afternoon, red-faced from the Wind Stone and grinning. I like that grin.
A slow afternoon is a gift. I spent mine watching a hawk below me circle the same hill a hundred times. It never caught anything. Neither did I.
Bees from the Cloud Garden come up to my nest every afternoon. I've decided they're visiting, not lost.
The shadows are stretching east across the clouds. In an hour they'll reach the next island over.
Afternoon is for little jobs: shaking out the cushions, picking burrs from my veils, telling the koi they're handsome.
The Market Pavilion is loudest after midday. Walkers bargain as if every emerald were their last.
Isn't it strange how the day feels heavier after noon? Not sad. Just full, like a cloud before it rains.
I'm in that warm half-sleep you only get in the afternoon, when the wind rocks you and the sun leans on your back.
I've had a tune stuck in my head since noon, and it isn't even one of ours. The wind must have blown it up from somewhere below.
{player}, you've got the afternoon look: too much sun and not nearly enough honey.
time.evening: There goes the dusk bell. In a little while the whole village will be over the Veil Court, veils out, voices up.
The lamplighter's going bridge to bridge now. Every lantern that wakes makes the next dark one look lonelier.
Look at the cloud sea. Rose, then gold, then grey. It changes faster than I can name the colours.
Whatever wind has the sky, Vell always sneaks in at dusk with a song tucked under its arm.
Miss the Evensong? I'd sooner miss supper. I've come to it with a torn veil and a streaming cold.
The walkers below are lighting their lamps. From up here the bell-villages look like a handful of glow berries dropped on a dark blanket.
Everyone's coming home now. You can tell who's tired by how low they fly.
I've been humming the low part all afternoon so I don't come in sharp tonight. Listen. No, don't, I'm saving it.
Dusk is the gentlest hour. Nobody hurries, nobody frets, and the sky does all the work.
Evening's the only time the gold thread in our veils really shows. Look at the edges, where the light catches: everyone's trimmed in sunset.
Walkers who've heard the Evensong say it rings in their ears for days. I hope that's a good thing.
The great lantern on the Spire is the first light lit and the last to go out. Somebody has to keep watch over the dark.
Sing the day down, we say, as if the day were a child who won't close its eyes without a song. I think it is.
Just at sunset the air goes still for a breath, every single evening. We all hold our veils out and wait for it to come back.
{friend} has saved me a place by the harps for the Evensong. The best place, if you don't mind being sung at from both sides.
time.night: Look up. The stars are so close tonight I keep tucking my veils in so I don't snag one.
Most of the village is curled up over their cushions by now. Listen: someone in the next nest is snoring like a sleepy harp.
Walkers see the stars through all that air. We're halfway to them already. They look near enough to pick like berries.
I should be asleep. But the night's so clear, and sleep will still be there in an hour.
Keep an eye out for night-moths. They come down out of the dark for walkers who've gone too long without sleep. You have slept, haven't you?
At night the cloud sea goes silver and the world below disappears. It's just us and the sky, the way it was at the start.
The chimes keep talking after everyone's asleep. I like to stay awake a little and listen to their gossip.
Night air carries everything. You can hear a harp three islands away, and someone turning over in their sleep.
My veils go loose and soft when I'm sleepy. Look at them, drooping. Mm. Where was I?
Some nights I try to count the stars over the Bell Pagoda. I've never got past the first hundred before I drop off mid-number.
Shh. The children are asleep in the nests, and children sleep lighter than veilcloth.
Night's when the sky gets bigger. By day it has a lid on it. At night it just keeps going up.
Out late, walker? Down on the ground you've got creepers and worse. Up here there's only the dark and the stars, and they're friendly.
One star sits over the Lantern Spire every night, in exactly the same spot. I've decided it's keeping watch with the great lantern.
{player}, you should be sleeping. Or is it the stars? They keep me up too.
time.late: It's the deep middle of the night. Only the wind and I are up, and the wind doesn't need the sleep.
I turned and turned over my cushion for an hour, like a koi chasing its own tail, and then I gave up.
This late, even the chimes stop talking. It's the quietest the sky ever gets.
Do walkers lie awake too? I always wondered if the ground holds you too tight to toss and turn.
When I can't sleep I fly one slow lap of the islands and count the sleeping nests. It never works, but I like the counting.
The dark before dawn is the coldest. My veils go stiff with it and I tuck my feet up under them.
At this hour the whole village feels like a dream somebody else is having.
Something heavy kept me awake. It's lighter now. Talking to a walker in the dark will do that.
The great lantern's still glowing over there, steady as anything. On sleepless nights I hover where I can see it, and somehow that helps.
It's so late it's nearly early. Another hour and the bell will ring, and I'll pretend I slept.
Late nights make me think of the ones who've gone up past the blue. I don't mind. It's a kind of visiting.
What are you doing awake? No, don't tell me. Whatever it is, I'm glad of the company.
In the small hours the cloud sea lies perfectly still. You could almost believe a walker might stroll across it to the next village.
Have you ever heard a skywood tree creak in its sleep? Only at this hour. It sounds like the island breathing.
I'm wide awake and I don't know why. My heart's high and my eyes won't close. Maybe tomorrow's going to be a good one.
weather.clear: Not a cloud above us and a whole floor of them below. Blue on top, white underneath: the best kind of day.
On a day like this, with the sun behind you, your shadow on the clouds wears a little rainbow ring. Walkers never get to see that.
Clear enough to see the wild islets from here. One of them has a tree I've never seen before. I mean to go and look one day.
Where the clouds break apart below you can see the ground through the gaps: green, brown, and a river like a dropped thread.
Sunlight on your veils with nothing in the way is like being held. Warm all the way down to the tips.
Blue in every direction. On days like this I forget there's anything below us at all.
Clear sky, clear head. I sorted out three worries before my first peach.
You can see the hawks working the fields way down there. From up here they're specks, and they think they're so high.
On a calm clear day the harps hardly stir, and the village goes so quiet you can hear the koi flicking their tails.
A clear day is a travelling day. If I didn't love this village I'd be halfway to the edge of the sky by now.
Fair weather for a walker to come up. You picked well. Last clear day like this we had six guests, and one wouldn't let go of the rail all afternoon.
The light on a clear day makes the gold in everyone's veils wink. The whole Veil Court sparkles like the koi.
The clouds below look solid as snow today. Every child tries to sit on one once. They come back up soaked and outraged.
The sky's so clean today it looks freshly woven.
I spent the morning on my back in the air, just looking up. There's nothing up there but more blue. It's wonderful.
Clear days are when you can spot a whale from furthest off. Keep your eyes east, walker. Maybe today.
Not a breath of trouble anywhere. The sky's in a good mood today, and up here moods are catching.
{player}, on a day this clear I watched you come all the way up from the Wind Stone. You wave like a walker: whole arm, very earnest.
weather.rain: It's raining on everyone below us. All that grey down there, and here we are in the light. I almost feel I should apologise.
This rain's falling past us from some cloud higher than the village. Rude of it. Rain is supposed to happen underneath.
I flew up through the rain to dry off. There's always sun above the rain cloud, if you're willing to climb for it.
From up here the rain hangs from the underside of the clouds in long grey threads that reach right down to the hills.
The Cloud Garden is drinking this in. The skywood leaves are shining, and the peaches will be fat by the end of the week.
The koi love rain. They dart at the drops like children chasing bubbles.
A wet veil weighs as much as a bad mood. I've been flying low all morning.
Rain at our height means the clouds have come up to visit. Everything goes soft and grey and close. It's like flying inside a sigh.
When the sun comes out after rain, a rainbow from up here is a whole ring, not a half. Walkers only ever get half.
Mind the bridges, {player}. Rain makes the skywood slick, and it's a long way down for anyone without a veil.
Rain doesn't stop the Wind Stone. Walkers came up the shaft wet as river stones and laughing about it.
On the veilcloth awnings rain makes a hush, not a patter. As if the sky were telling everyone to whisper.
The harps hate rain. Wet strings go slack and sing everything a little sad.
Best sleeping weather there is, rain below us. The cloud sea goes thick and dark and soft, like a bed nobody's allowed in.
Rain caught up high tastes of nothing, clean as a new veil. By the time it reaches you, it's picked up the taste of everything it fell past.
I think an Old Singer is behind this. One went by singing low last night, and here's the rain.
The children are flying in and out of the drops, trying to dodge every one. Nobody's managed it yet. Nobody's stopped trying.
Everyone's tucked under the awnings with their veils wrung out and dripping. It's the only time you'll see a Cirri keep still.
weather.thunder: Did you hear the bell ringing on and on? That's the storm peal. When it rings like that, everyone goes home and stays home.
Lightning looks for the tallest thing in the sky, and up here the tallest thing is us. Please don't stay out in it.
Thunder isn't a sound up here. It's a shove. It goes straight through your chest and out the ends of your veils.
The children are all tucked in the nests with someone humming to them. Humming covers the thunder, a little.
The harps go wild in a storm. Somebody ought to still them, but nobody dares fly to the Hall of Echoes in this.
I saw a bolt strike the cloud sea below us once. The whole cloud lit up from inside like a lantern. I didn't sleep for two nights.
Somewhere behind all that, Borre is laughing. Storms are Borre's idea of a joke, and nobody else finds them funny.
You walkers are lucky in a storm. You can crouch in a cave, and the lightning can't find you down there.
Stay close to me if you're staying at all. I'm not much, but two in a storm are braver than one.
Every Cirri knows what to do when it thunders: home, curl small, tuck your veils in and hum. Even the eldest.
Sorry, I'm jumpy. Every rumble, my veils snap tight around me. They're more frightened than I am, and I'm very frightened.
The Ruined Belltowers were struck again and again before they sank, they say. Iron bells call the lightning down. One more reason we build light.
Not a day for soaring. The sky's all teeth today.
The whales dive deep into the clouds when it storms. Even the Old Singers won't sing over thunder.
When it's over, the air will smell sharp and new. That's the one good thing about a storm, and I'm waiting for it.
Talk to me, {player}. About anything. Your caves, your fields, the things walkers eat. Something with no thunder in it.
Thunder rolls along the top of the cloud sea like something heavy being dragged. I hate heavy things. I hate this most of all.
Poor walkers in the bell-villages below. Though I'd rather have a stone roof than a veilcloth one tonight, I'll admit.
weather.snow: Snow! Up here it doesn't fall so much as wander. Sideways, upward, round about, as if it hasn't made up its mind.
Snowflakes catch in my veils and stay. By evening I'll be wearing the whole winter.
Snow is the only weather slow enough to talk to. Hello, flake. Goodbye, flake.
The koi have gone slow and dreamy in the cold. They hang over the pool like lanterns somebody forgot to light.
Frost on the harp strings. They ring higher in the cold, thin and sweet, as if they're singing through their teeth.
You can see your breath, {player}. Mine too. Look: little clouds of our own.
White on top of the islands, white in the cloud sea below. Without the sun you can't tell up from down.
I've wrapped my feet in veilcloth. Bare feet and snow are not friends, whatever the children tell you.
The children are catching flakes on their tongues, and then on each other's veils, and now it's a war.
Everything's hushed. Even the chimes sound like they're whispering.
The skywood trees are all wearing white. The gardeners are out shaking the branches so they don't crack under it.
My veils have gone stiff as bark in this cold. I'm flying like a dropped plank today.
Down through the cloud sea goes every flake, and vanishes. I like to think of each one landing on some walker's roof.
Walkers love snow, don't they? Your feet leave marks in it. Ours never leave a mark on anything.
Walkers come over the snowy bridges sliding and yelping, and we hover alongside and cheer.
I had a peach so cold it crunched. Don't tell the gardeners. They'd be scandalised.
The Bell Pagoda's roof has a cap of snow like a sleepy hat. Every time the bell rings the whole cap slides off at once, and every time I laugh.
Snow makes me want to curl up over my cushion with honey and a story. Do walkers have snow stories? Tell me one.
moon.full: Full moon tonight. It's so close and round I keep wanting to knock and see if anyone's home.
The moon's paying us a proper visit. Look below: every cloud in the sea has gone silver.
On a full moon even the great lantern looks a little embarrassed.
The koi love the full moon. They rise high over the pool and turn their sides to it, all shining.
Too bright to sleep. I've been hovering with my eyes shut and I can still see the moon through my eyelids.
Round as a sky peach tonight. If it came any nearer I'd take a bite.
A full moon and not a breath of wind. The whole village is one big silver stillness.
{player}, look at your shadow on the bridge. Moonlight this strong makes even a walker look light enough to fly.
moon.waning_gibbous: The moon's lost a sliver off its edge since last night. Somebody's been nibbling.
A little less moon tonight. It goes the way a good guest leaves: slowly, and looking back.
The moon rises later every night now, like a neighbour who's taken to staying out.
Still bright enough to see the koi by, but one edge has blurred, like a veil seen through rain.
When the moon starts to shrink I always feel a little low. Then I remember it comes back. It always comes back.
The moon's leaning to one side tonight, lopsided, as if it's listening for something.
A walker once told me the moon is just a big rock. A rock! I laughed so hard I lost height.
Look at the shadowed edge. You can still see where the round of it should be, if you squint and want it badly enough.
moon.last_quarter: Half a moon tonight, the other half resting. I know just how it feels.
The moon's cut straight down the middle, like a nest door left half open.
Half a moon, half a sleep. That's the rule on nights like this.
The moon's showing us its back tonight. It's on its way somewhere, and it won't say where.
A half moon is the honest one. Half bright, half dark, and not pretending otherwise.
With only half a moon, the faint stars come back. Look at them all, crowding in round the edges.
Make your promises on a half moon, my elders taught me: there's light enough to mean them by, and dark enough to keep you humble.
Half a moon and half a village awake. I'm in the awake half, it seems.
moon.waning_crescent: Just a thin curl of moon tonight, like the frayed tip of a veil.
The moon's nearly gone visiting. A few more nights and it'll be dark for a while.
A thin moon and a big sky. The stars have the run of the place tonight.
Look closely and you can see the rest of the moon, dim and grey, held in that thin bright curve. Like a sleeper in a blanket.
The moon's so thin it barely lights the bridges. Walk carefully, walker. You're the only one of us who has to.
We call this the moon's last bow. It bends low and thin, and then off it goes.
The night-moths like a thin moon. I keep close to the lanterns till it fattens up again, and I hum.
When the moon's this thin I miss it already, the way you miss a friend who's started packing.
moon.new: No moon at all tonight. Our neighbour's away, and the sky feels emptier for it.
Dark moon. The stars are so thick tonight it looks like someone shook out a veil full of frost.
On a dark moon the great lantern is the brightest thing for miles. Walkers below must think a star came down to stay.
The children don't like the dark moon. I tell them the moon is only resting its eyes, and it is.
Without the moon you can't tell where the cloud sea ends and the sky begins. It's all one dark, and we float in the middle of it.
No moon means a good night for counting stars and a bad night for finding your nest. I've drifted into two wrong ones already.
The Old Singers sing louder on a moonless night. Maybe they're calling the moon home.
Every time the moon goes, it comes back. In the dark, I find that a great comfort.
moon.waxing_crescent: There's the moon, just a thin smile low over the cloud sea. It's back!
A sliver of moon tonight, sharp and bright as a new harp string.
The first thin moon is lucky. You make a wish on it, quietly, and tell nobody. I've just made mine.
The moon's a little hook tonight. If I could reach it I'd hang a lantern on it.
The moon's coming back a bit at a time, careful, like a walker on the bridges for the first time.
Look, the moon's peeking round the edge of the dark. Welcome home, neighbour.
The koi saw the moon before I did. They were all turned west, waiting for it.
A growing moon is for beginnings, we say. I've been meaning to begin something. Maybe tonight.
moon.first_quarter: Half a moon and growing. Every night it fills a little more, like a cup of nectar under a dripping flower.
The moon's lit on one side and dark on the other, like a face turned half toward a lantern.
A half moon early in the night always looks like it's hurrying to catch up with the sun.
Half a moon makes the best shadows. Look at the bridge rails, drawn across the cloud like a ladder.
Half a moon is plenty to fly home by and not so much it keeps you awake. It's my favourite.
The moon's like a peach cut in two tonight. Somebody's saving the other half for later.
I'm halfway through something too, I think. Like the moon, I'm hoping the second half is the bright one.
The children say a half moon is the moon winking. Since they told me, I can't see it any other way.
moon.waxing_gibbous: Nearly full. Another night or two and the moon will be round as a nest.
The moon's bright enough to weave by now. Long ago the weavers worked right through such nights, before there were lanterns on every bridge.
Almost full, and everyone's restless. The koi, the children, me. The moon does that.
A fat moon, not quite finished. It looks like it's holding its breath.
The cloud sea's already glowing. Wait till it's full: you'll see your own shadow on the clouds at midnight.
There's a lumpy little piece missing off one side of the moon, as if somebody's still making it.
The moon's on its way to full, and there's always good news on the way to a full moon. Something's coming. I can feel it in my veils.
{player}, you've come up on a good night. The moon's nearly full and the whole sky is showing off.
wind.aure: Aure has the sky today. Gentle as a hand on your back. You barely have to fly at all.
Flying in Aure is like flying through a morning that won't end: damp and soft, smelling of dew and new leaves.
Dew all along my veils, strung there by Aure. When the sun catches it I'm wearing a hundred little lanterns.
Cloth woven on an Aure day stays soft forever, the weavers say. The Loom House has been busy since first light.
Aure is the neighbour who knocks so softly you're never sure you heard. Then you look out and the whole step is wet with dew.
Even the children fly gently in Aure. It's hard to be wild in a wind that kind.
The harps play so quietly in Aure you have to lean in. It's the only wind that makes them whisper.
Out of the east, out of the dawn itself: that's where Aure comes from. Some days it still smells of sunrise at noon.
Nothing much happens on an Aure day, and I like it that way. Nobody tears a veil. Nobody shouts.
Look at the clouds: still pink at the edges, hours after sunrise. Aure carries the dawn's colours along with it.
When I was small they always put me up in Aure to practise. It catches you when you wobble.
Of the four winds, Aure's the one I'd marry, if winds married. Gentle, early, and never once in a temper.
A whole day of Aure and I've done nothing but drift and hum. Do walkers have days like that?
So damp, this wind. The koi swim higher than usual, right up into it, as if the air had turned to water.
Aure never blows long at a stretch. It sighs, and rests, and sighs again, like someone settling into sleep.
wind.sefa: Sefa has the sky today, warm and lazy. You don't fly in Sefa so much as let it carry you wherever it was going anyway.
